speechtext:
Hon. J. E SINCL.AIR (Queens, for Mr. Kay) presented the ninth report of the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization, as follows:
The select standing committee on agriculture and colonization begs leave to submit/ its ninth report as follows:	,
Your committee have had under consideration a resolution and order of reference dated February 16, 1928, whereby it was resolved:
That whereas the protein content is an important factor in the value of wheat,
"Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house, the National _ Council of Industrial and Scientific Research in conjunction with the Board of Grain Commissioners be asked to investigate and report on the feasibility of utilizing the protein content of wheat as a basic factor in the grading of that product.
And further be it resolved that this resolution be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization for consideration and for such suggestions in connection with the grading and inspection of wheat as it deems advisable to pass on to the said national council and Board of Grain Commissioners."

Grading oj Wheat-Report of Committee
Pursuant to the said resolution and order of reference, your committee has agreed to the following conclusions, which it has passed on to the said national council and the Board of Grain Commissioners, viz:
1.	From a price standpoint baking strength is an important element in wheat, and in the Canada Grain Act definitions of our higher grades, baking strength is determined by two factors-variety and percentage of hard red vitreous kernels.
2.	In the resolution submitted to your committee it is proposed to amend the Grain Act so as to determine baking strength by the two factors-variety and quantity of protein-the latter to be determined by a chemical test and to be expressed in percentages.
3.	In Canada, Great Britain, the United States and probably most other countries that consume Canadian wheat, baking strength is an important factor in determining its value; by strength is meant the quantity and quality of protein.
4.	Except in the case of durum wheat, which at present is graded in a class by itself, and possibly one or two other varieties that are grown in relatively small quantities, the protein in the contract grades can be assumed to be of good quality.
5.	All things considered, the amount of gluten, that is, of protein, seems, in the light of present day knowledge to be the nearest approach to an ideal index of baking strength available.
6.	The cost of making the protein tests would range from 50 cents to 75 cents, and is not considered a serious difficulty notwithstanding the fact that laboratories would necessarily have to be installed at all inspection points. We would suggest that data be obtained as to cost of installing and maintaining laboratories.
7.	The time required to make an individual test would be from one and a half hours to two _ hours. However, as daylight is not required for laboratory testing, and as a large number of tests may be conducted simultaneously, under sufficient organization operating 24 hours a day, no difficulty would be encountered in testing of cars and no delay in despatching cars to terminal points may be anticipated.
8.	The definite proposal contained in the resolution could be put into effect in so far as car-lot shipments are concerned, but your committee is not yet satisfied that wheat sold locally in wagon-loads could take advantage of this scheme. A practice in vogue among members of the Kansas wheat pool whereby the farmer and elevator man forwarded samples jointly to the laboratories would seem to point the way to a solution of the difficulty concerning street wheat and this system should be investigated.
9.	The introduction of protein as a factor in wheat grading would be an incentive to grow the best milling varieties of wheat. This we consider of great importance.
10.	According to Mr. L. H. Newman, Dominion cerealist, Ottawa, and in the opinion of this committee, the following varieties are classed as desirable:-Early Red Fife. Marquis, Ruby, Red Bobs, Selections, Renfrew, Kitchener, Garnet and Reward.
11.	It is highly desirable that the cereal division of the federal Department of Agriculture, and the several provincial governments working jointly, continue in their efforts to zone Canada's wheat area with a view to advising as to the variety, or varieties, most likely to prove satisfactory in each case.
12.	So far however, as our export trade is concerned, there was not sufficient evidence submitted to the committee relative to the effect of the proposed change in the basis of grading to warrant your committee recommending its adoption at present. However, your committee recommends that a full enquiry into this phase of the question be instituted.
13.	Re: Garnet wheat-In so far as evidence would show we are of the opinion this wheat which has hitherto been excluded from No. 1 northern should be eligible for that grade.
14.	Re: Complaints of Liverpool Corn Trade Association.
Your committee believe that the complaint in the matter of No. 3 can be in some measure sustained, due principally to the inclusion in this grade of a large volume of improperly dried wheat.
Respecting the complaints regarding the general lowering of the standard of respective grades other than No. 3, we find that the evidence does not bear out this complaint.
Regarding the situation with respect to No. 3, we find that the Board of Grain Commissioners and the department are now fully alive to this situation. We recommend that steps be taken to prevent a continuation of this condition.
^ We recommend that the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Board of Grain Commissioners keep a careful check upon the quality of export wheat, and that samples of export shipments should regularly be secured and sent to the chief inspector and retained in his office for purpose of comparison; and also that the laboratory be required to make baking tests _ and report on samples of shipments regarding which complaint has been made.
15.	The committee recommends:	(a) temporary interchange of inspectors between the several inspection points in the western division.
(b) Uniformity of standards of grades from year to year is most necessary and for the purpose of comparison standard samples should be preserved for at least five years.
16.	In order that the high quality of our export wheat be maintained, and in order to discourage, as far as possible, the growth of undesirable varieties of wheat, we would urge that one or more seed warehouses be estab-lished^ for the purpose of collecting and distributing seed of approved varieties, and that an experimental flour mill of sufficient size be established in order that experimental work in milling and baking may be conducted on a scale that will give results in line with those obtained in commercial mills.
The committee would suggest that the cost of construction and equipping these facilities may well be taken from surpluses of revenue over expenditures in the administration of the Grain Act and the revenue from terminal elevators overages in the western inspection division.
17.	The committee recommends that the protein map prepared by Dr. Birchard, exhibited to the committee, be printed for distribution and that a similar map be prepared by the research laboratory for distribution as early as possible in each year.
18.	This committee recommends that inspectors be appointed at all transfer points between the head of the lakes and the seaboard, whose duty it will be to prevent any mixing of wheat so that the quality and condition of grades as fixed by final inspection will be maintained.

Mr. C. R. MctINTOSH (North Battleford): I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Neill:
That the fourth report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations be concurred in.

There is just one word that I should like to say in regard to this report and to draw it to the attention of the Prime Minister and the government. I am not objecting to the main sentiment expressed in the report. I think the real intention of the report is simply to indicate that there is a problem and that it should be further studied. I gather from reading the whole report that was really what the committee had in mind, but in section 2 there is a very positive declaration:
That we accept and endorse the principle of unemployment insurance.
The point I am drawing to the attention of the Prime Minister is this. It is quite true that in the subsequent paragraph that declaration is qualified by pointing out that the matter is within provincial jurisdiction and there are one or two other qualifications. For instance, the committee indicate that there is an insufficiency of data to determine to what degree unemployment exists and the committee are also unable to make any estimate of the cost. Such qualifications follow the declaration, but in my opinion a declaration of this kind going out from parliament with its unanimous endorsation will convey to the public at large the impression that parliament has endorsed and consequently will be

bound to implement by legislation a definite unemployment insurance scheme. That I think would be misleading. It ought to be made clear that such a declaration by parliament at this time is limited by the obvious limitations indicated in the subsequent paragraphs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I agree with my hon.
friend that if it were to 'be assumed that the report carries with it an obligation on the part of the government to implement by legislation any of its resolutions or expressions of view, it would not be advisable that the report should be endorsed by the house. The government regard the statement with respect to principle as purely and simply an expression of opinion and, having regard to other phases of the report not as one imposing any obligation on the federal administration.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Wininpeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I think anyone who has read the report will recognize that whilst certain limitations are expressed with regard to the immediate adoption of the principle, whilst according to the law officers of the crown the obligations primarily rest with the provinces and whilst we have not yet sufficient information to enable us to work out a scheme, there is also in the report the opinion of the law officers that it is quite possible for us in regard to unemployment insurance to follow the lines already adopted in regard to old age pensions. Therefore it seems to me that we are not going very far in adopting this report, when, after all, we are committed under the treaty of the League of Nations to put into legislation unemployment insurance. I think that principle of unemployment insurance was adopted by the Conservative party at their last convention at Winnipeg and I hope the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is not going back on the platform of his party. Then, may I suggest to the Prime Minister that if endorsing the report does not mean that we are going to implement it 'by legislation, we may as well kill the report to-day. We do not want to go on giving the public the impression that we are going to do something-forever expressing pious resolutions and then failing to implement them. Although I am tremendously in favour of getting something on the record with regard to unemployment insurance, if this report means simply another pious hope on the part of the government that something will at some time be done, let us to-day kill the resolution for concurrence and then the public will know where the government stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Reading the report of the committee I find the following:
That the evidence of the Justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities, it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act, but that it would be within the power of parliament to contribute, by grant, to such provinces as adopted such legislation, following the precedent set in the matter of technical education, highway construction, and, more recently, the Old Age Pension Act.
Then I find that section 7 states:
In order that this matter might be further dealt with, your committee recommends to parliament that at the next session this question be again referred to the committee on industrial and international relations.
I have no objection at all to adopting this recommendation. It is made clear that the matter is a provincial one. Of course the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a little aggressive in these matters. He would like us to enact legislation which would not be within our jurisdiction.
If the hon. member will permit me, it is also made clear by the report that it is quite competent for parliament to proceed along the lines followed in connection with old age pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To help; to make grants. That is why the committee has reported that the matter should be further dealt with at the next session of parliament.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see why we should have such an outburst on the part of the hon. gentleman.

The point is simply this. If I understood the Prime Minister aright, he was going to interpret the report that there was no obligation whatever to implement it by legislation, and I take the ground that if the report means anything, it means that we should study the problem further with a definite view of enacting legislation. If the government is not prepared to take it in that way, the government ought to make that very clear now so that the country at large can understand the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I made my position clear to my hon. friend. If he assumes that in passing the report at this time the government is obligating itself to ask the house to vote money for unemployment insurance-
No.

speechtext:
-he should
understand clearly that the government would not support the report.
No, I did not suggest that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the
point I wish to make clear.

I
think it was thoroughly understood by the committee and, I hope, by the house, that this is merely an interim report and an interim report does not carry with it any insistent demand for legislation or action forthwith by the government except to carry out the recommendations contained in the seventh paragraph that investigations be continued next year and to obtain data asked for in paragraphs five and six. I do not think it will hurt the house or the country to accept and endorse the principle. I would point out that this is no new thing. As far back as 1919, the Union government, I suppose, brought together a national industrial conference of Dominion and provincial governments with representative employers and labour men, on the subjects of industrial relations and labour laws', and for the consideration of the labour features of the treaty of Peace. That conference sat for quite a while and went very thoroughly into all phases of the question. I find that they report on some sixteen items, and the third item reads as follows:
We recommend immediate inquiry by expert boards into the following subjects, with a view to early legislation:
(a) State insurance against unemployment, sickness, invalidity and old age.
That recommendation was adopted. If that was the opinion of this conference in 1919, that an immediate inquiry should be made with a view to early legislation, I do not think we are veiy much ahead of the times when we ask, nearly ten years later, that we endorse the principle of unemployment insurance.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I desire to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that on the 18th of May, speaking in this house in answer to a question, he stated to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that it was erroneous to assume that the British government could not sign the treaty of peace known as the Kellogg treaty without the concurrence of the Dominion. But on the 19th of May, Sir Austen Chamberlain, in a letter to Mr. Kellogg, stated that the treaty because of its very nature could not be participated in otherwise than jointly and simultaneously with the dominions' and India-a seeming contradiction to the Prime Minister's statement. That in itself was serious, but on the following day, May 20t.h, Sir Austen Chamberlain in a further letter to Mr. Kellogg, intimated that because England had certain interests in unspecified territories throughout the world, she would sign the treaty only on the distinct understanding that it did not prejudice her freedom of action in respect to those territories and her interest therein.
I now desire to ask the Prime Minister, because of the obvious commitments and moral obligations implied in the reservations made by Sir Austen Chamberlain, whether he would be willing to agree that this house shall have an opportunity of discussing the treaty before its ratification, and secondly, would he care to give the house a statement as to his acceptance or otherwise of the Chamberlain reservations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend, I would say first with respect to any alleged conflict of opinion between Sir Austen Chamberlain and myself, that I do not think there is any, I was speaking with respect to the policy of the Canadian government as to the signing of the treaty, and I indicated that, having regard to conditions of which we would wish to take account on the invitation being extended to us we would be quite prepared to sign. Sir Austen Chamberlain was speaking with respect to the position of the British government, and announcing its policy. The British government is free to pursue whatever course it wishes with respect to signing the treaty. It may have reservations which it will widh to make, and which it has a perfect right to make. As I say, Sir Austen Chamberlain has given the point of view of the British government, stating its

Civil Service-Poslal Employees
policy with respect to the invitation extended to it. I have given our point of view with respect to the invitation as extended to Canada.
As to the treaty being submitted to parliament for approval, if my hon. friend has looked over the correspondence, as I am sure he has, he will have noticed that in the reply sent to the United States, our government intimated that the treaty would be submitted to parliament for approval before ratification was recommended.
With respect to the last question of my hon. friend, as to whether this government would express any dissent or approval of the reservations suggested by Sir Austen Chamberlain, I consider that is a matter with which the British government itself should deal. I do not think we are called upon at this time to give any further expression of our views.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Postmaster General what action has been taken in regard to the salaries of railway mail clerks and also refer him to the promise he made some time ago in relation thereto?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Already within the last two weeks, Mr. Speaker, I have answered that question twice. But I was further asked if the commission had given any reasons why they did not carry out the recommendations of the Postmaster General as to the increase of salaries of postal helpers, postal clerks, mail carriers and railway mail clerks, to which I answered that I had received no reasons from the commission. Since that time, however, the commission has seen fit to give reasons through the Secretary of State, and with the permission of the house I will read the reasons, which will clear up the whole situation. The letter received by me previous to this was dated May 22, which I read to the house at the time. This is dated May 23 and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Rinfret,
In view of the discussion which took place in the House of Commons on Monday last with reference to the refusal of the Civil Service Commissioners to recommend higher rates of compensation for certain classes of employees in the postal service, the Civil Service Commissioners have prepared a brief explanation of (heir action therein, and would be pleased to have you make this explanation to the house.
On September 19th, 1927, at the request of the Civil Service Commission, the Deputy Postmaster General submitted the following suggestions with regard to maximum salary for certain classes in the postal service:
Postal clerks in grade 6 post offices and up- maximum $1,800 per annum. Present salary range $1,080-$1,740.
Postal clerks in post offices of grade 3 to grade 5-maximum $1,680 per annum. Present salary range $1,080-$1,620.
Letter carriers-maximum $1,560 per annum plus uniform and boots. Present salary range $1,080-$1,500 plus uniform and boots.
Mail porters-maximum $1,560 per annum. Present salary range $1,080-$1,500 plus uniform and boots in certain instances, and at a later date suggested an increase of $60 in maximum for the class, railway mail clerk, or a new maximum salary of $1,860, the present salary for which class is $1,080-$1,800 plus mileage.
The commission has been giving attention to the question of salaries for Post Office and Customs department classes almost continuously since April, 1924, and has in this time increased the maximum and minimum salaries for all of the classes $240, the revision of 1924 granting an increase of $180 and the revision of 1927 an increase of $60 per annum, the letter carrier receiving an extra increase of $60 in the minimum.
The commission believes that the salaries paid this class of employee are equitable and comparable with other salaries paid for somewhat similar kinds of work in other government departments and feels that if any increase is recommended for the postal classes that a corresponding increase must be recommended for Customs classes and certain classes in the Department of Immigration and Colonization, as well as for a considerable number of other classes in other departments of the government service who are engaged in work of a nature *not much different and carrying as great responsibility as that of employees in the Post Office Department.
In the opinion of the commissioners it would be entirely unfair to the Customs, Immigration and other employees with somewhat similar kind of work to perform to recommend higher rates of compensation for the postal classes without making recommendations for higher compensation for the classes in which these employees are classified.
To increase the postal employees' salaries an amount of $60 in minimum and maximum would create an additional estimated expenditure of approximately $550,000, and the additional amount required to include Customs, Immigration and other classes throughout the service which, m the opinion of the commission, should participate would cost approximately $400,000 or a total increased expenditure of $950,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
In view of the various objections which were made by members of the house, I am going to suggest that one of my colleagues move that this vote be reduced to $200,000, and that it be made conditional upon the wharf being at the disposal of the public. My information is that all boats travelling in that channel are permitted to use that wharf. It is very important as a place of shelter, and I have found, on making inquiries since the vote was up before, that about 347 vessels used it last year. This figure may not be correct as I have not the details available, but it is a very large number.
There was the further abjection raised by my hon. friends from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) and Quebec South (Mr. Power) that the public did not have access to this private property. I think hon. merrfbers in every section of the house will understand the difficulty there is in dealing with a situation of this kind. Until 1926 this property was not utilized for anything except pleasure purposes. Since that time there has been a development there, and I think every member who considers the results derived from it must consider that it has been in the best interests of the country as a- whole. The arrangement at the present time is that 420,000 cords of pulpwood will be removed each year. Last year there were 300,000 cords removed, and a little less than that the year before, but the arrangement is that 420,000 cords will be removed this year and each subsequent year. It is thought that the growth will amount to 450,000 cords, according to the estimates of

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
the men who tramped over the area at the time of purchase. Objection has been taken to the fact that it was a privately owned island and the people who were there had not the right a British subject should have to go back and forth at will. That is largely a matter for the provincial government, but I feel that we should say to the company that we expect them to obtain for the people who are engaged there the privileges which a British subject should have. I do not think it is an unreasonable request that some hon. members of the committee make that a substantial part of this vote should stand over until another year. In the meantime, what is granted will be conditional upon the public having the use of the wharf.
Is it the intention to export any of this pulpwood across the line?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The arrangement with the three paper companies, two at Three Rivers and one at Port Alfred, is that this pulpwood will be made into paiper at these three Canadian mills. Since the matter was before the committee before I have gone into it in a good deal of detail, and I find that the expenditure for wages during the calendar year 1927 amounts to about $2,000,000. They pay the bushmen $75 per month and board and housing in the lumber camps. They have expended nearly an equal amount in the purchase of supplies, largely from Canadian farmers. The paper to be made from this pulpwood at these three mills will run to a value of around $20,000,000 per year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When this vote was last before the committee the member for East Calgary moved that the vote be reduced by $290,000. The question is on this amendment.

I have listened to what the Minister of Public Works has said, and I want to assure the committee that my amendment to this vote was not with the purpose of obstructing. All the discussion that has taken place, except at the present time, has been on the questions of revenue or profit, what business would be brought to the Dominion of Canada, and what revenue might be paid to the Dominion exchequer. What caused me to be so greatly interested in the matter was the utter absence of any provision for preserving the rights of the people living on the island. It is a fact that the habitants on the island, as my hon. friend from Quebec South has pointed out, have absolutely no rights as Canadian citizens. They have to buy their stores from the company at whatever prices the company sees fit to ask. Be-fMt, Elliott.]
fore I can go on to the island I have to ask permission and my business is inquired into. It is a perfect example of a benevolent Mussolini autocracy. It is quite true that the company maintains private hospitals, schools, and so forth, but it taxes the inhabitants for them and the latter do not enjoy any of the ordinary rights of Canadian citizens. The Manchester Guardian has this to say about the island of Anticosti:
Technically, Anticosti is part of Canada's domain. It is part of the county of Saguenay in the province of Quebec. But its island isolation and its exclusive ownership give it some of the qualities of an independent kingdom.
It is a kingdom within the Dominion of Canada.
In practice the control exercised by the federal authorities is casual and meagre. On Anticosti there is the autocratic government of private ownership that brooks no popular rule. The inhabitants of the island are there on sufferance; they have no voice in its rule. There is a closed door beside which that of China gapes by comparison. The Anticosti Corporation is a law unto itself; it permits entry or prohibits landing at will.
In view of the benevolent Mussolini organization which controls the island, I cannot support any grant to the corporation on the mere statement of the minister that he expects it to do so and so. I want to know first that the inhabitants of the island have the rights which they are supposed to enjoy under the British flag. The company who own the island have the Canadian flag flying over it. They like it for their own protection; they like it because they are going to get some grants of money, but the inhabitants of the island are deprived of what I would call Canadian rights. We in this corner of the house are occasionally criticized because we are analytical and critical in regard to various things and we are told that we have no constructive policy to offer in matters of this sort. Before I sit down I want to give the conditions under which I might support any grant to the island. I will not support it on the statement of the minister that he will tell the company: We expect you to do so and so. I want to know that it is being done before one dollar more of Canada's money is handed over to the corporation which owns the island. I am glad to see that the Minister of Public Works has taken into consideration the question of the right of any Canadian vessel to enter that harbour and to use the wharf subject to whatever government dues there may be, if there are any. It is not good enough for me to have the Minister of Public Works state that he will request or expect the company

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
to do so and so. I must 'be satisfied that the inhabitants have the rights which Canadian citizens enjoy. Therefore I make four propositions and if they are accepted and1 put into force I shall be prepared to support a grant of $100,000. The propositions are as follows:
1.	That all vessels shall have the right of use of the harbour and wharf, paying dues as per government schedule, if there are any. The minister has provided for that.
2.	That the district known as the residential part shall be surveyed and incorporated as a town in the province of Quebec, not as a private town owned by a private company but as an incorporated town with all the rights of a town.
3.	That the residents of the aforesaid residential district shall have the same rights and privileges of self-government, free speech and assembly and industrial organization as Canadians enjoy in any other town in Quebec.
4.	That as far as that part of the island known as the town is concerned, any person shall have the same free right of entry as to any other Canadian town.
In other words, when I visit Quebec or Montreal I enter as a Canadian citizen and I am not questioned as to what I want there. I have the right to go there and any Canadian citizen should have the right to visit that town and to transact business there without being questioned or, if the company do not like him, being told to make himself scarce. If they expect a grant of Canadian money-and the inhabitants of the island are contributing part of that money by their work-I would suggest that all the inhabitants should have the same Canadian rights as we have. If these conditions are imposed and enforced before a dollar of the grant is paid over, I will support the grant, but otherwise I cannot support it.

I know it has
been the policy of the Public Works department under both administrations to give assistance to companies that have started enterprises on navigable waters. I know of several rivers in Quebec where enterprises have been started and work given to the public and where there has been need of dredging or building wharves to carry on the business. In such cases the Department of Public Works has been in the habit of giving assistance in that connection and, I think in most cases, quite proper. But I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in nearly all of these cases the work is going on in a place where people are already living and where the land is owned by various people
and not all by one company. I consider this Anticosti island is in a class by itself. The island is owned entirely by the corporation and I do not see any public interest to justify the Department of Public Works in paying part of the expenses of doing that business. These companies are powerful companies who are doing good work; they have bought the island purely for private gain, and the construction of wharves and the dredging done at the island are entirely for their own use. The public get no use out of this at all. It seems to me that the company ought properly to stand all the cost required to enable them to develop the resources of the island and to take the pulpwood away. I do not see why the Department of Public Works should vote all this money for purely private purposes. There is no other object in this expenditure than to enable these companies to make money out of their pulpwood and therefore it seems to me that the minister is going in the wrong direction. I do not think the precedents of other votes to enable enterprises to get started apply in this instance at all. Further than that, as I understand the matter-and if I am wrong the minister will put me right-this island being entirely private property, works built on it will really belong to the company. That is to say, nominally they will be the property of the Dominion government, but as a matter of fact they will be used only by the company except in a few instances such as the minister has mentioned where they may be used for shelter in case of storm. Therefore I see no justification for any of this vote. It is purely for the purpose of putting money into the pockets of the people who own the island.
May I ask the minister if any money has previously been expended on Anticosti island at Ellis bay for harbour or dredging purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The amount spent by the company runs close to $2,500,000. The company built the wharf entirely at their own expense. It is an excellent wharf, and as the engineer says, it is so situated that:
This development scheme will be a great aid to shipping in the gulf of the St. Lawrence as it is proposed to make Ellis bay the provision centre for ships in the gulf where coal and fresh water will be obtainable at the new wharf. There will also be adequate protection for shipping in bad weather and a sea-going tug will be kept on hand to render assistance to ships in distress in the gulf.
What my hon. friend says about assistance in other cases is quite true. For years back the government has endeavoured to encourage

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
development along proper lines of industrial activity, either by building the wharf and doing the dredging, with the company bearing part of the cost, or the company building the wharf and the government doing the dredging. But in this case the cost of the wharf is so much out of proportion to the cost of the dredging that the department, after very careful consideration, decided that it was only fair to do the dredging. It is to be done in the main channel of the St. Lawrence, and the company itself has no jurisdiction in the channel; it could not do the dredging. The work is also of value, as I have said, from the standpoint of a shelter for ships in that part of the St. Lawrence, which as my hon. friends all know is a pretty difficult part so far as navigation is concerned. I am told that last year one boat was able to avail itself of the shelter of this dock, with the result that possibly the lives of the crew on the boat, numbering twenty-eight, were saved, so that it is valuable from the standpoint of protection to those who have to travel these waters. The fact that the company have expended $2,500,000 made the department feel that it was not doing any more in this case, nor for that matter bearing as large a proportion of the general expense, as has been done in other cases. I think this is good business; it is a development that should be encouraged, and I think the company is doing a fair proportion of the work.

Possibly the minister
did not quite understand my question. I know personally that this company has spent a considerable amount of money on the island for wharves and other purposes, but what I wanted to know was if the Department of Public Works had already spent any money for harbour or dredging purposes on the island.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No, except what has been done under this contract last year.
What was the amount spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The amount of work that has been done is $187,000.
What is the total amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Just about half a million
dollars.

The Minister of Public
Works has dealt with certain aspects of this question, but has not touched upon one or two points that have been raised by the hon.

member for East Calgary which are of great importance to this country, and on which he ought to give us a little more definite assurance than he has so far done this morning.
At the present time there are no public highways in Anticosti. I understand that the island is about the size of the whole province of Prince Edward Island, and that the owners of the island could debar anyone from walking in any part of that large domain. There are no public health regulations, and no laws pertaining to sanitation. All these questions are of vital importance. There is no such thing as law and order on that island, and so far as law and order is concerned it can be run just as suits the company best. I think under these circumstances, before one cent of assistance is given by the government, we should receive the definite assurance from the minister that all these matters !l have mentioned will be looked after and put on the same footing as in other parts of Canada. I believe also that the owners of the island control the landing privileges, and consquently the landing of vessels there would depend on the goodwill of the owners of the island. That is not as it ought to be. If we are going to give grants, we ought to have something to say as to the wages that shall be paid and the working conditions that shall prevail. I believe that the company could, if they wished, and it has been done in other parts of the country, prevent a man going on the island to organize the workers into what I might call a legitimate trades union. Company towns in Canada have done that .within recent times; and we migffit find that a person who wanted to land on the island would get no farther than the wharf. I want him to have permission to go to any part of the island, just as he could to any part of the city of Montreal or the city of Quebec. I wish the minister would rise in his place and assure the house that none of this money will be granted by the government until they have the assurance from the owners that all these matters will be put on a proper footing.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As a representative of the district where the island is situated, I want to say just a few words. The hon. member for Argenteuil has pointed out that, after all, whatever is done on this island is done for the pecuniary benefit of the company which is operating on the island. Well, that applies to all companies. Companies are not philanthropic associations; they are in business for a profit, and this organization on the island is in the lumbering business for

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
the purpose of making a profit to be distributed among its shareholders, just like any other company in Canada.
The dredging which the government is now proposing to do is necessary in order to connect the main channel in the river St. Lawrence with the wharves of the company. These wharves were built and paid for entirely by the company, and if my information is correct over one million dollars has been expended by the company for new wharfage accommodation. Is it reasonable after a company has gone to that expense that the government of Canada should disregard that large industrial development, and refuse to do anything whatsoever in assisting in that development, when the government does it everywhere else in Canada? If the government refuse, there is no other authority except the authority which lies with this parliament and with this federal government to do that dredging. No private corporation can dredge in the river St. Lawrence.
Could they not dredge with the consent of the government?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Probably they might, but would that principle be adopted by parliament? Could the principle be defended before this house of allowing private individuals or private corporations to start dredging in the river St. Lawrence? It is a public channel.
Under the control of the government, I said.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it would be a good principle to allow individuals to start dredging in the river St. Lawrence, which is the most important channel of navigation we have. This has to be done by the government.
Why?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Why? In the same way that we cannot allow individuals to do construction work on railways. Our railways, as well as the river St. Lawrence, have to be under the control of a central authority.

Was not that principle adopted by the government in the case of some survey work last year in northern Manitoba, where the government did the work but the bills were paid by the Manitoba Paper Company, which would profit by the survey?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It might be so; but my hon. friend would not for one moment compare surveying territory in Manitoba with allowing private corporations to dredge in the river St. Lawrence and interfere with navigation.
Why not?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Now, Mr. Chairman, the question has been raised of this island being private property-
Could not the work be done by the government and be paid for by the company?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; that principle was adopted somewhere else. We made arrangements with other companies whereby the government paid two-thirds of the cost of the work and the company one-third. But, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Public Works, in this particular work the company has already expended over two million dollars in building wharves. In the other instances where the cost of the dredging was shared by a company and the government the wharves as a rule were built by the government itself.
A moment ago the minister said it was done for profit not for philanthropy.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I mean lumbering is a commercial enterprise; there is no doubt about that. Now, as to this island being in the hands of a private company. Well, first of all we must bear in mind that that company bought the rights of Senator Menier. The senator derived his rights from the Coffin estate. This island of Anticosti is in a seigneury.
The feudal system.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have to take things in this country as they are. We have other seigneuries in the province of Quebec.

Is that Liberal
doctrine?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is not my fault if three hundred years ago the king of France granted seigneuries;-
But there is something to be said-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: -and there is such a thing in this country as vested rights.
We understand that is Liberal doctrine too.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend for one moment contend that on account of a special system of land tenure having been

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
established in this country over three hundred years ago, we are to change that now? Coming to my last point, I want the members of the committee to bear in mind that in the case of land tenure we immediately enter a field which is altogether provincial. We cannot do anything even if we wanted to. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) mentioned "Liberal doctrine". There is one principle of Liberal doctrine that he will subscribe to-the autonomy of the provinces. Well, if we are to respect provincial autonomy we have to keep away from property and civil rights.
Does the hon. minister suggest that the principle of autonomy means that we have to make this grant?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend is putting that question seriously.

I am putting it
seriously. Let me ask the question this way: Simply because a king of France three hundred years ago granted a seigneury, does it mean that now industrial development has taken place we in Canada must make money grants to a company which is attempting to exploit that island?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I am not arguing in favour of this grant because the island is a seigneury, but I am answering the argument of my hon. friend that before we do any dredging we ought to change the land system on this island. I say we cannot change it because it is not within the competence of this parliament. The provincial government has sole jurisdiction as to property and civil rights.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the conditions on this island are not as bad as they have been described, for if they were people would not go there. If the people were treated in such a way as to recall feudal days, as has been said in this house, how could they be induced to go and work there? The people are absolutely free to go or not to go. No one can force them to go and work on that island if they do not want to.

Economic necessity drives
them to work there.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No economic necessity will drive people from the province of Quebec, as I know them, to become slaves. I am aware how the business on this island is carried on. Every fall when the people leave the city of Quebec to work on the island they go there as free men, and they come back as free men.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to interrupt, but may I ask the Solicitor General a question? I quite understand that people are not obliged to go to the island against their will; but can anybody go there without a pass from the company?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.
Is anybody permitted to land there without having a permit or pass from the company?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly; over three hundred vessels went there last year.

That does not
answer my question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How could three hundred vessels go there if people were not allowed to land?
They got permits.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has experience in the lumber business-
I should like an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I will answer the question. My hon. friend has had experience in that line of business. Would he contend for one moment that the holder of a license to cut timber in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario, even though he is not the owner of the soil, would allow the public generally to roam through his limits and endanger them? He would not. It is not done anywhere. My hon. friend knows that. Timber holders protect their property. Why should not the owners of Anticosti protect their property also?

What civil rights
have those workmen from Quebec on Anticosti island?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend that the people of Quebec protect themselves and their rights.

That is not an
answer to my question. I ask:	What civil
rights have the workmen from Quebec on Anticosti island?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They have the same rights as other labour men throughout Canada.
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The provincial government of Quebec would not allow to. prevail on the island the condition of things which has been described in this house and in certain newspapers. That is not the kind of government we have in Quebec.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers

Are the conditions
described by the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) wrongly described?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
To a certain extent they
are. My hon. friend from Quebec South has experience in the way timber companies conduct business. He knows that whaJt the people at Anticosti do is simply to protect t'heir property as every other company does. I am fully confident that should the employees of that company consider themselves not treated as they ought to be, as regards municipal organization or otherwise, they know what to do. They have one authority to whom they can appeal any time, any dby, any month, and that authority is not the Dominion parliament; it is the provincial legislature and the provincial government, the government of the province of Quebec. And knowing the prime minister of the province as I know him, I have no doubt justice will be done to the people of Anticosti as justice is done to all people in our province. Moreover, if the people were not satisfied either with this government or with the provincial government the courts of the province are there to protect the rights of all citizens; and what shows that conditions on the island in no way approximate the conditions that have been described is the fact that no action ever has been taken at any time in the courts by anyone.
How far away is Anticosti island?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Anticosti island is not at the north pole; it is in the district of Charle-voix-Saguenay. We have an organization in Quebec which extends throughout the province and these people are not isolated. I submit these facts: First, we are doing for this company what has been done for others in many instances; secondly, as regards the amount, as the Minister of Public Works has suggested, it might be reduced to cover the work actually done this year; thirdly, the proper authority to deal with the matter is the provincial government and the provincial courts and not the federal government; and in the fourth place, speaking from my own personal knowledge, you will never find people from Quebec going to work on that island to become slaves, for they would not go there if the company did not treat them properly.

I want to
congratulate the Solicitor General on the over-shadbwing influence of his very strong and aggressive personality on the Minister of Public Works. He is entitled to that tribute, and I only wish I could enlist his services in regard to another island which happens to be situated
in the St. Lawrence river, which is opposite Kingston, and which is known by the name of Simcoe. That little island is peopled by a population entirely of farmers. A couple of years ago when the ice on the St. Lawrence went out it carried away their wharf and since that time they have been asking, and I have been asking on their behalf, for a little consideration in order to have a wharf built to enable vessels to come in there and give the farmers of the island some service. For the last two years the farmers of the island have been unable to market their stock, their hay or anything else until nature has provided them with a bridge by freezing over the river. In the summer months they cannot get off at all. The people of the island have not been asking for $300,000 nor $100,000 nor $1,000. They sary, " If you will give us six or seven hundred dollars we are so anxious to have the wharf, which means so much to us, that we the farmers of the island will give our own work gratis. Let the department send their man down to supervise the work and we will not ask pay for what we do in building the wharf ". All these people ask for is six or seven hundred dollars. Can I get the ear of the government in that respect? Can I get any assistance from the hard-hearted Minister of Public Works? He does not look hard-hearted, but he is apparently extremely hard-hearted and absolutely callous, indifferent and hard-shelled, unless someone with the engaging personality of the Solicitor General can approach him, and then they can get anywhere up into six figures for anything at all, no matter where it is. But the farmers on that island have received no consideration whatever from this government. This government can tear down half the city of Ottawa to satisfy the ambitious whims of the right hon. the Prime Minister to make a monument for himself in the shape of what I suppose we shall in years to come call King's park. The government can give hundreds of thousands, millions in that way but the farmers on this island cannot even get six or seven hundred dollars to put up a wharf to enable them to market their produce in summer. They must wait until the ice comes and the good Lord provides them with a bridge so that they can get off the island. But $300,000 is nothing in Anticosti, away in the gulf, where even ordinary citizens are restricted in their rights to go and come, everything being under the control of one corporation. The government can spend this money now' to provide them with what they need, and when the timber is cut off the island they can move off. I should not

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
be doing my duty if I did not point out to this committee and to the house the absolutely unfair position which the government has taken in regard to some of these small amounts which are rightly asked for by people in various parts of the Dominion. No consideration whatever is given these demands. It is not a question of the rights of the case; it is a question of these people having sent to this parliament a member who sits on this side of the house instead of on the other side. That is the long and short of it; that is the size of it; that is the big and little of it, and it is mostly little.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When my hon. friend made his unkind reference to myself I was on the point of getting up to support him. I think he has made a fairly strong case for the people of whom he speaks, and if I can be of assistance to him I shall be glad to do what I can.

When I paid a tribute to the Solicitor General I appreciated his influence and his engaging personality. But if I am to have the assistance of the right hon. the Prime Minister, then I must say, with all due deference to the Solicitor General, that I should prefer help from the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I did not say they only had the rights of other timber limit holders. I said they had greater rights, but I compared the way the ordinarj' timber limit holder with inferior rights treated the general public.

I understood the Solicitor General to say that ordinary persons were not permitted to cross the territory of timber limit holders in the province of Quebec. Having been connected for a long time with people who were timber limit holders and having brought my hon. friend fishing within those limits. I know that they permit certain kinds of people to cross their limits at all events. Perhaps that was because I was with him, but at any rate I must say that the rights of timber limit holders in the province of Quebec are not the feudal rights exercised by the Anticosti Corporation.

In addition to hearing the foregoing witnesses your committee took under consideration resolutions and petitions submitted by various organizations throughout the country.
Your committee begs leave to report its conclusions and recommendations as follows, namely:
Conditions under which Citizens of various Countries are admitted to Canada
The committee is convinced that there is considerable misapprehension and lack of information regarding conditions on which persons from different parts of the world are admitted to Canada. In order to remove this misapprehension and to have a clear background on which to base any recommendation, the committee gives the following brief summary.
British
1.	All British subjects from the United Kingdom or from any of the British dominions are eligible to enter Canada, provided they are sound mentally and physically and in a position to maintain themselves until employment can be secured.
No passport is required.
The passage rate for immigrants from the British Isles generally is $91.25.
2.	British agricultural workers are specially encouraged by the establishment of a low rate of $9.73 at the instance of the Canadian government.
3.	British domestic workers are also provided for at the same rate as agricultural workers and in special cases even this small amount is advanced as a loan.
4.	Families of British agricultural workers who have already emigrated to Canada are given the benefit of the special rate of $9.73 for adults and free passage to all children under seventeen. In this case, also, loans are made in special cases to provide for the transportation of such families.
5.	British children over fourteen and under seventeen who are brought into Canada under the auspices of certain juvenile societies, have their passages paid; and an additional amount is paid to such societies to cover the railroad fares and incidental expenses of such children.
6.	British boys over fourteen and under seventeen years of age, emigrating to Canada to approved farm homes, receive free passage to their destination.
Northern European Countries - (Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Switzerland, Holland, Belgium and France).
Any subjects or citizens of these countries are eligible for entry to Canada provided they are sound mentally and physically and are in a position to maintain themselves until employment can be secured.
These people are required to have passports.
The average minimum ocean rate is approximately $120.

No special rate or assistance of any kind is given by the Canadian government to subjects or citizens of these countries.
Central and Southern European countries- (Austria, Hugary, Poland, Roumania, Lithunia, Esthonia, Latvia, Bulgaria, Jugo-Slavia, Czechoslovakia) .
Only agricultural workers, domestic servants or those within a prescribed degree of relationship to residents already legally admitted to Canada are permitted to come in from these countries. Special exceptions may be made in cases in which the Minister of Immigration is satisfied that their labour or service is required in Canada.
These people are required to have passports.
The average minimum ocean rate is approximately $135.
No special rate or assistance of any kind is given by the Canadian government to subjects or citizens of these countries.
United States.
All citizens of the United States are eligible to emigrate to Canada provide they are sound mentally and physically and in a position to maintain themselves until employment can be secured.
No passport is required.
From the above it will be seen that emigrants from the United Kingdom stand in a specially favourable position as compared with emigrants from continental countries, not only with regard to general passage rates but particularly with respect to the very greatly reduced rates given to agricultural and domestic workers from the United Kingdom.
For the further encouragement of British immigration the following schemes for land settlement should be noted:-
3,000 Family Scheme.
British families have been brought out to Canada at a special steamship rate, and they are located by the Canadian government on vacant soldier settlement lands. The British government supplies to each such family a maximum of $1,500 cash for stock and equipment. All repayments are made by the settler for the price of the farm and for the stock and equipment loan, in equal yearly instalments, during a period of twenty-five years at the low interest rate of 5 per cent. The Canadian government provides additional assistance by way of selection, settlement and supervision, free of charge.
British-Dominion-Provincial Land Settlement Scheme.
Under this scheme the provincial government provides the farm. The British government supplies $1,500 for stock and equipment. The Canadian government recruits the settler and provides settlement and supervision, free of charge, and, in addition, shares on a 50-50 basis any loss on account of stock and equipment. In the event of the default of a settler within the first two years the loss of interest on account of the purchase price of the land is shared on
the following basis:

This scheme has already been adopted by two of the provinces and negotiations are now being carried on with another province.
Training and Placement of British Boys in Farm Homes.

Selected boys are given free passage from the United Kingdom to Canada, and institutions known as "training farms" are established by several provinces for receiving these British boys and distributing them among approved farm homes. The Dominion and provincial governments each contribute $10 per boy towards the operation of the farm, and the British government makes a grant of $20 for the same purpose.
Land Settlement for British Boys.
The object is to establish on farms of their own, British boys who have come to Canada, and who have acquired the necessary experience in farm work, and who have each saved $500. Under this scheme the British government loans $1,250, the Dominion government $1,000, the provincial government $250 and these loans, with the boy's savings, aggregate $3,000 which is available for his settlement on the farm.
To indicate the importance of this work the British and Canadian governments have entered into an agreement to spend $5,000,000 during the next ten years in making such loans.
As illustrating the special efforts put forward to encourage British immigration, the evidence shows that the Canadian Department of Immigration spends in this work $16.67 for each British immigrant as compared with an average cost of 11 cents per head for immigrants from the continental countries.
The committee heard evidence in detail respecting the organization of the Department of Immigration, and concerning all phases of its activities as carried on both separately and in conjunction with many governmental and voluntary organizations, and in relation thereto the committee makes the following recommendations and suggestions.
Federal Responsibility.
In the opinion of the committee the responsibility and control of the selection of immigrants, no matter by whom recruited must rest solely and exclusively with the government of Canada.
Provincial Co-operation.
The committee recommends that special efforts be now made to extend the field of activity of the provincial authorities particularly in the matter of placement, settlement and supervision of immigrants, and that, with this in view, the federal government consider contributing to defray the cost of provincial co-operation for that purpose.
Medical Examination
There have been complaints about the new system of medical inspection under which Canadian doctors conduct the medical examination of prospective immigrants in the United Kingdom. It appears that this new system was inaugurated as a result of representations made to the Department of Immigration by steamship companies, by provincial governments, by the Dominion Council of Health, and by other social service organizations.
Several reasons were urged in favour of the change:
1.	Great hardship was imposed on the immigrant who had been passed by the medical inspectors in the United Kingdom and then upon coming to Canada was subsequently rejected on arrival or after admission.
2.	A large number of deportations have taken place on account of the mental or physical w

Immigration-Report of Committee
fitness of those who had been passed as mentally and physically fit before leaving the United Kingdom.
3.	The proportion of immigrants committed to mental institutions in Canada has been excessive.
The new system affords free medical examination of prospective immigrants by Canadian doctors before they take passage for Canada. Twenty-one Canadian doctors and forty-five roster doctors are conducting medical inspection in the British Isles, and there are 332 centres where medical examinations are conducted, and, in addition, special provisions are made for medical examination in isolated communities.
On the continent there are seven Canadian doctors whose work is confined to examining all immigrants at the continental ports of embarkation. Previous to this examination by Canadian doctors the continental immigrant is subjected to a medical examination near his home under the auspices of the steamship company. Quarantine, fumigation and other precautions are exacted at the continental ports of embarkation in addition to the medical examination by the Canadian doctors.
The suggestion was made that the volume of emigration from the British Isles to Canada was being reduced by the new medical arrangement, but the evidence showed that there has been a greater decrease in emigration from the British Isles to the other overseas dominions and to the United States.
The committee was impressed with the fact that the_ medical officers to whom is entrusted the medical examination of intending emigrants have a serious responsibility to Canada, not only to the federal government but also to the provinces. It is their duty to ascertain that intending emigrants are physically and mentally fit to take their places and do their share as Canadian citizens. In this connection, and more particularly with regard to immigration from the continent of Europe the committee quotes the resolution passed by the Social Service Council of Canada at its meeting recently held in Montreal as follows:
"The Social Service Council of Canada having in mind the burden now laid on the various provinces^ of Canada in providing for the idiots and the insane, and the unfortunate results of admission into this country of the moron and feeble minded, desires to urge upon the federal government a continued and strict adherence to the provisions of the Immigration Act, in order that the door may not be open for the entrance of these types of prohibited undesirables."
_ Owing to the present arrangements a considerable amount of misunderstanding and dissatisfaction has arisen during the transition period. Certain objections were mentioned by witnesses, some of which have already been 'remedied. The present system of medical examination in the British Isles was inaugurated primarily for the benefit and protection of the British emigrant. The Department of Immigration and Department of Health should, it is considered, make the most exhaustive efforts to see that the new system is perfected so as to eliminate, as far as possible, inconvenience, delay and expense to the prospective emigrant, and to dispel the idea that there is any intention, on the part of the Canadian government, to restrict or hinder the coming to Canada of British subjects. For this
purpose the committee recommends that the present system would be improved and that it would obviate delay and inconvenience to the prospective emigrant, especially those who reside in the rural districts of the British Isles, if the medical examinations were made by British local doctors paid by, and under the supervision and control of, the Canadian medical authorities, who should be located at convenient centres of population.
Special Passage Rates for British Settlers
1.	'Teen Age.
The Committee approves of all previous efforts to promote and encourage 'teen age immigration from Great Britain and recommends that the age limit for boy immigrants be extended to boys 14 to 19 years of age, both inclusive.
2.	Domestics.
That the arrangements now in effect for the movement of domestics from the United Kingdom to Canada be continued.
3.	Family Re-union.
That measures be taken to extend the assisted passage privileges to the families of immigrants from Great Britain who are now in Canada and who have so far established themselves as to have a reasonable prospect of being able to support their families in this country.
4.	Reduction in Ocean Rates for all British
Immigrants.
That measures be taken at an early date to arrange a conference between the federal and British governments and the Atlantic steamship companies with the object of obtaining a reduction in ocean rates to British immigrants to approximately £10.
Railway Rates for Canadian Landseekers
The committee also recommend that measures be taken to ascertain whether the railways will restore the home seekers rates in effect prior to the war. making such rates effective east-bound as well as westbound.
Land Settlement
1.	The committee having heard the evidence in connection with the experiment of the 3,000 Settlement Scheme, now almost completed, recommend that time be given to test this form of land settlement before embarking upon extended schemes of this character.
2.	The committee approve of the extension to other provinces of the tripartite agreement with the British, federal and provincial governments for the encouragement of land settlement by the British emigrant.
3.	The committee recommend, subject to the completion of satisfactory arrangements with governments of the provinces, that assistance equal to that given by the British government to British emigrant boys be extended by the government of Canada to the Canadian youth who are trained in agriculture.
Letters of Assurance of Employment "Permits"-so-called
Your committee recommend that letters of assurance of employment shall state the names, addresses, occupations and nationality of the persons to be admitted and that an annual return be made by the Minister of Immigra-

Railways' Continental Agreement There was in the evidence, considerable criticism of certain features of the railways' agreement. The committee has some doubts as to the desirability of giving to the railways special authority to recruit immigrants, but as certain restrictions were imposed in connection with the renewal of the agreement in October, 1927, the committee is of the opinion that in order to ascertain the results of its operation under the ne\v conditions, the present agreement might be continued according to its terms, but with this exception-that the system of nominations of immigrants from non-preferred countries under the railways' agreement should be confined forthwith to the following degrees of relationship; father or mother, husband or wife, son or daughter, brother or sister of any individual who is now engaged in farming in Canada, and further that the existing railways' agreement should not be renewed in its present form.
Increasing Employment Your committee would also recommend that the government make an intensive and comprehensive study of the possibilities of increasing industrial and agricultural development in Canada with a view' to attracting capital and providing wider and increased opportunities for employment not only for our own people, but for prospective immigrants.
Your committee recommends that 1,500 copies in English and 500 copies in French of the minutes of evidence and of this report, be printed in blue book form and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.
A copy of the minutes of procedure and evidence is appended hereto for the information of the house.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Chairman.
