They were not able to finance the undertaking, but are hopeful that they wifi be able to do so and to repay the government. We took it over but were only able to instal the machinery necessary to carry on, get it all in shape and move the plant across the railway track, and put in the switch necessary for convenient loading. The staff anticipate being able to commence operations this year with a full force, and I hope they will operate the plant during the whole season. We will not require as much money this year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What are the company's obligations; if I remember right, there was an agreement.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The original agreement was for the purchase of the site then existing, and carrying on the work in rented premises. They could not make a satisfactory agreement with the proprietor, and since that time we have purchased property across the railroad tracks. We now own that bog by direct purchase.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What did you pay for
it?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: $5,150 is the purchase price. We hope to manufacture this season in a commercial way and establish this industry on a commercial basis. We also hope that the company will be able to finance it and take it off our hands.
How much money was spent last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: Was there any production?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Mr. Chairman, when I
referred to this matter last year the minister

Supply-Mines
was very emphatic that important results were going to be obtained during the last twelve months. This bog has been a sink of iniquity for a great number of years. There has been more lying done about it, not by the minister but by others connected with it, than perhaps any other single enterprise this government has undertaken. The minister need not think that he will ever make a commercial success out of operating this peat bog; it is not possible to do it. Peat cannot be dried commercially so as to get a new dollar back for an old one. Wherever peat is used the world over it is only by the local people, who spade it out, stack it up and air-dry it. Peat contains a very considerable amount of moisture that cannot be evarporated or driven out by heat or in any other way, because it is microscopically combined with the peat itself. That is a fact that I have no doubt the minister knows as does everybody else who has had experience in handling peat in a scientific way. Why continue this farce of endeavouring to operate something that cannot be done commercially? I am at a loss to understand why the minister persists in doing that. The late Doctor Haanel wrestled with this matter for nearly twenty years and got nowhere. The minister will get nowhere and no department on earth can make a success commercially of this matter. Why then persist in the endeavour?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
One can
never tell of course until the experiment is completed.
There are some scientific facts that speak for themselves and cannot be disputed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
After investigating almost every process, we have come to the conclusion, just as my hon. friend has stated, that there is only one process that shows any possibilities of success and that is air-drying by spreading a comparatively thin coat over the surface of the ground. One primary difficulty that we have to overcome is the moisture in the air in this locality. I confess that is rather a serious proposition; it is serious to the extent that it curtails the output. We have all the machinery in place; we have the electric current there to carry the experiment to a conclusion, and we hope to manufacture peat this year. But of course I am not going to say for a moment that if we have a very wet summer we shall get a large quantity of peat, because the quantity depends on how fast you can dry it. The Danish process is about to be put into effect at Sherbrooke,
Quebec, entirely independent of the government. They have the machinery on the ground; they have spent some money on the project, so that I think that is a fair indication that they mean business. I want to carry the experiment to a conclusion and to demonstrate whether or not peat can be manufactured successfully. I admit at once it cannot be Shipped any great distance because it is too bulky.

The department have
been struggling with this matter for a number of years and the minister will admit they have never got anywhere.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Well, he may as well admit it, because there is no question that is the fact. The reports from his department covering a period of ten or fifteen years point to that fact, and he admits that the only process of dealing with peat is by air-drying. The amount of labour you have to put on the material is more than the commercial value of the product after it reaches the consumer. That is all there is to the matter. Where peat is being used it is being used by the residents or natives of the country digging it for themselves and air-drying it. In other words, the cost of labour is not included. It is not a commercial matter; it is simply a domestic affair. The people in the immediate locality could probably do the same thing. The peat will not bear transportation or working by any method, mechanical or otherwise, that the minister may employ provided he pays the ruling rate of wages. The minister will be forced to come back when we review the matter next year and admit that the result of his operations is that just as much money has been lost as was the case in former years. Perhaps some other people are now trying the experiment in Quebec, if that be so they will have a similar experience to that of the minister.

I do not propose to criticize the vote. What I want to know is this. Supposing the operations are successful at Alfred, does the minister know of other places in Canada where the process can be applied successfully?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes,	I
know a peat bog near my old home in the vicinity of Holland Landing, a very fine bog. There are any number of bogs.
In Alberta?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, in Ontario. There are any number of bogs in

Supply-M ines
Ontario. Some of them may not be as adaptable to working as the one at Alfred, but there is no question about the quantity of peat if we can develop a process for handling it.
Has the minister any information in regard to the western provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Is the minister aware of
the experiment carried on or the amount of money expended in Welland and Wellington counties in connection with the very process he is speaking of, namely, the air-drying process of producing peat? A very large expenditure was made there and the same company has spent a great deal of money in this section in the very bogs that I think the government are working on to-day. In view of the failure of private capital in this respect, the government is very foolish to continue the work.

I am afraid I cannot agree with the views of some hon. gentlemen on this side who have spoken in regard to the matter, My reason for taking that stand is that there are in the county of Frontenac bogs which give great promise along this line. Some people there are interested and they have a right to look forward with hope to something being done which will make their property of real value in this regard. One or two in Frontenac county have written me in regard to the operation at Alfred and they are anxiously awaiting the result of the government's investigation into the peat proposition in that part of Ontario. I am interested in the experiment, largely because of their interest, and I think everyone will agree that in Ontario if we could handle the peat in a way that would satisfy some of the demands of the public, it would be of great value in a province which has no coal. There may be and likely are similar properties in Quebec. These provinces have at present only the white coal, that is the water-power, to depend upon. They are certainly at a disadvantage in having no coal and I would not be doing my duty in regard to this item if I did not give it support and look forward with hope to something being done w'hich will prove of real value to the development of similar properties in the constituency which I represent.

The vote
under consideration is one that has occupied a good deal of time in the house in the years
'Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
that have passed. Frankly I never understood why the experiment was started in the first place. Even if fuel that could be used was developed from these peat bogs, its light weight, bulkiness and cost of transportation to any great distance would make the use of it almost prohibitive. Therefore outside of areas within the vicinity of the bogs themselves there would be little hope that this peat fuel could be put to any general use. Moreover, because of the nature of the fuel, the low heating value of it, it would be of use only in the fall or spring months of the year. In fact I think the minister himself is reasonably convinced of the truth of that statement. I have however no desire to impede the passing of the vote at this stage, if, as the minister says, he now having set up this plant and having certain equipment there, merely desires to complete the investigation. I would like to ask the minister how much more money will be required to complete this infernal investigation which has been going on now for so many years without anything in the way of concrete results whatsoever.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is not
any more infernal an operation than the one we started at Bienfait. I should not say I started it, but I had the honour of trying to complete it. Notwithstanding the fact that we have spent $1,000,000 of good hard cash of this Dominion on that experiment, which was said to be a failure, there is construction of a plant going on there, not to utilize exactly the same process as was evolved, but nearly the same process. By a high temperature process we are going to carbonize coal at that mine, and make out of what is a comparatively low grade fuel a rather high grade fuel in a territory where there is no fuel of that character. We cannot say that any experiment of this kind is going to turn out a dead failure. All I have to say is that we have purchased all the machinery, we are going to operate the plant at Alfred, and we expect it to carry itself this year. So far as we are concerned we intend to demonstrate,^ by costs and otherwise, in this year's operation, what peat can be produced for, what it can be sold for, and whether it can meet the competition in an area beyond one hundred miles of coal coming in from outside sources for fuel purposes, at least in the fall and in the spring, when there is a market for a reasonable quantity of this fuel.

Are we to
understand that the minister means the vote granted this year will complete the experimental work?

Supply-M ines

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is for
operating the plant.

No more
money will be asked for next year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not unless
we have to operate the plant next year, and I hope not, because I am hoping that the company will take it over. I am informed that to-day the plant is turning out one hundred and sixty tons of fuel. That will be sold, and we will recoup ourselves, but we need money to carry on.

Was there
any revenue from the plant last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We did not manufacture any last year. We were buying new machinery and buying the peat bog, and it was all outlay on plant and equipment.

Is there a
blue book report on the operations thus far which I could get? I should like to have a publication of that kind.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There will
be. I would not say that it is in print, but it can be produced and printed for the use of hon. members.

How much of that $1,000
for transportation charges on ore shipments was spent last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not one
dollar, I am sorry to say. As my hon. friend knows, that was put in the estimates as a result of the agitation for the construction of a plant in British Columbia, which we did not consider advisable at that time. We had in the estimates at one time an item of $10,000 I think, for the purpose of transporting samples of ore from British Columbia and
all outlying points in Canada to Ottawa for testing purposes, but advantage has not been taken of that appropriation. We did not spend one dollar of it last year.

I would remind the minister that there is in the township at Wainfleet, in the county of Welland, an area of peat bog of several thousand acres. It might be well to investigate the possibilities there.

I would ask the minister
if under this vote an amount is appropriated for subscriptions to periodicals and newspapers?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: Has the minister a record of the amount expended by his department for subscriptions to newspapers and periodicals during the year 1927.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have not
a detailed statement here.

According to a return that was tabled in the house, I find that the Department of the Interior, including Mines and Indian affairs, took under the heading of newspapers, 213 publications and paid for 296 subscriptions, and under the heading of "other publications" took 673 publications and paid for 912 subscriptions, at a total cost of $7,499.14. Included in these figures were 145 subscriptions to daily newspapers. It appeared to me that there was an evident lack of proper supervision, not only in this department, but in every department of the government, with respect to expenditure along these lines, and in order to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of the Interior and of ministers of other departments I would lake to give the figures for each department now, rather than bring them up when the estimates of the respective departments are before the committee for consideration:

That makes a total cost for subscriptions to newspapers, periodicals and trade journals of $32,762.34, not including those for the reading room. It is difficult to determine from the Auditor General's report what is allotted to each department for subscriptions to newspapers and periodicals, but I find in this return that in the Department of Labour there is an increase for 1927 over 1925 of $445.57; and there may be increases in some of the other departments.
I fully appreciate the necessity of subscribing for newspapers and trade and technical journals, but I fail to see any reason for buying so many copies. For instance, in the Department of Agriculture I find the following: Manitoba Free Press, 13 copies; Montreal Gazette, 12 copies; Montreal Star, 6 copies; Toronto Globe, 7 copies; Farmers' Advocate, London, 67 copies; Northwestern Farmer, Winnipeg, 32 copies; Farm and Dairy, Peterborough, 22 copies; Farmers Sun, 19 copies; Grain Growers' Guide, 32 copies; Canadian Official Railway Guide, 18 copies; Family Herald and Weekly Star, 15 copies- and also one copy of Canadian Sports and Daily Racing Form. Presumably the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is preparing for the races. In the Department of the Interior I find the following subscriptions to newspapers and periodicals: Calgary Herald, 6; Edmonton Bulletin, 7; Edmonton Journal, 4; Lethbridge Herald, 4; Vancouver Daily Province, 5; Manitoba Free Press, 11; and so on; Financial Post, 4; Saturday Night, 5. In all departments of government I find, aside from the reading room, the subscriptions to daily papers number 1,200. As an example: Ottawa Journal, 136; Ottawa Citizen, 116; Manitoba Free Press, 77; Montreal Gazette,

105; Montreal Star, 53; Toronto Globe, 68; Toronto Saturday Night, 32; MacLean's Magazine, 22.
As I stated a moment ago, I fully realize the necessity of subscribing for a certain number of newspapers and trade and technical journals. But when we go home and attempt to explain to some of our constituents that we cannot get a rural mail route established, or that we have not sufficient money to furnish them with anything better than a tri-weekly mail service, and they know that the various departments of government are subscribing for 1,200 copies of daily newspapers, it will be hard to explain to them why the postal service should suffer. I bring this to the attention of the minister and his colleagues in the hope that they will look into the matter.

Referring again to the
Alfred peat bog, I find last year we spent altogether $22,898.27. This included $4,353 for land, leaving $18,545, of which labour costs represent only $1,876 and a few cents. In other words, over nine-tenths of the expenditure is overhead.
Rent and salaries.

I will come to that in
a moment. The manager gets $6,000 a year, and his clerk is in receipt of $1,260 odd. But the entire labour bill is only $1,876. How can any enterprise of that character stand such a disproportionate overhead? The Irishman at home spades out his peat and there is no overhead. In no other way can this fuel be used economically. Now let me refer to another matter. I understood the minister to say he was doing some briquetting in the west.

Supply-Mines

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not now.
Where?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Bienfait,
Sask.

You have abandoned
that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes, four
or five years ago.
I congratulate the minister on his display of good sense as to that matter. I hope he will do the same with regard to the Alfred bog, and the sooner the better.

Two of the main
activities of the department, I notice, are in connection with the explosives division. Is the department doing anything beyond the inspection of explosives?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is the testing of explosives by Colonel Ogilvy. There is also the inspection of the explosive plants, but this is not done usually by him, unless there is some special reason; ordinarily the work is attended to by the mounted police, who look after the safety of the public in connection with this inspection.
How many explosive companies are operating in Canada at the present time, or have they all been bought up by the Americans?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are twelve factories operating in the Dominion.

On page 3 of the
report the beneficiation of iron ore is dealt with. Has any practical result come from this research work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is a rather lengthy report which I shall be glad to give to my hon. friend. It goes into details showing what is being done. Without reference to the report, we must confess that we have not got very far with the development of new treatments of any sort. Investigations have been carried along old lines.

I shall be glad to get the report. In my opinion, as I have pointed out before, there has been a want of co-operation; the government has not paid sufficient attention to these reports. Was the minister really carrying out his free trade principles, or was he discharging his function as minister of the mining department, when he allowed the Robb budget to bring in all these products required for insecticides and so on? Here are two or three reports which
deal with the importance of these things, especially with reference to arsenic. The very products from our own mines which enter into these insecticides and fungicides are brought in from the United States. This report, which gives a survey of Canada, was intended to locate the arsenic areas in Canada, but with the introduction of these products from the United States our research work has practically stopped. The minister might support this change in the tariff by arguing that it was not a matter of price, but I think he will agree with me that as these byproducts of the smelteis are used up, and in view of the fact that one-third of the supply of arsenic comes from these smelters, in proportion as this material is consumed in the United States and we have abandoned research work, the price is bound to rise. There is no question about that. At one time, when arsenic was used less extensively as an insecticide, it was a drug on the market; it was very cheap. But as it came into use the price rose. If we are not busy locating and making use of our own supplies in Canada the price will go up. Therefore the minister should be intensely active in the development of our own ores and the products which will provide us with a supply of these commodities. It is worth while calling attention to that fact. These reports are being published, book after book, and nothing is being done, notwithstanding that a great deal of expense is incurred. Money is being spent without producing the results intended for the development of our own industries.

An hon. member asked a question with regard to these publications. He put some very valuable information on the record this afternoon, and I am sure the minister himself must possess a huge fund of interesting material which he would like to divulge to the committee in regard to papers, periodicals, and so forth that come to his department. Here is one publication known as the Journal of Heredity. I do not know whether this is one of the publications in the minister's department, but it is printed in Washington. There are seventeen of these. Does this "heredity" refer to a certain type of gentlemen, the aristocracy of Canada, or has it reference to animals? I do not know whether the journal of heredity concerns itself with two-legged or four-legged animals. I should like the minister to take us into his confidence and let us know whether his department is spending money to furnish all the staff with these various publications.
Supply-Mines

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will wait until we come to the Department of the Interior, but if there are any in the Mines department I shall be glad to give him what information I have.
I presume you have a number of publications in the Mines branch.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Quite a
number.
Is that to provide the various members of the stall each with a copy?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

The number seems unnecessarily large. Possibly it is not, but that is the way it strikes me. The minister did not give the reason for such a number when my hon. friend behind me gave the information he did.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who previously spoke with reference to the matter had in mind newspapers that were coming in for use in the department. I believe he said that twenty newspapers came into the Mines department. I cannot say that this should be considered an excessive number because every day information must be available to various officers in the department. With respect to periodicals, this department occasionally uses a great many. The exchange of new ideas in almost every line of metallurgy in which the officers of the department are interested is invaluable, and of course it would necessitate aocess to everything that is going on throughout the world in the way of new development and the evolution of new ideas. I am unable to tell my hon. friend why it is necessary to have twenty newspapers in one department. However I will inquire into the necessity for that number.

With regard to the supply of arsenic, which is coming into the country in increasing quantities all the time, I would suggest to the minister that instead of whipping dead horses, as he has been doing in the briquetting of coal, and endeavouring to do the impossible so far as peat is concerned, he might turn his attention to the question of utilizing our ores in Canada in relation to the supply of arsenic. It is estimated that there are in Nova Scotia 100,000 tons of tailings containing a considerable percentage of arsenic. The hon. member for Kingston has referred to the output of the smelters, and has asked what is being done by the department with regard to the 
investigation of that matter, which is certainly of vital importance to the country at this moment. A large market is assured to-day and we are depending entirely on our neighbours for that supply.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is no question about the quantities of arsenic available in Canada. It does not need a geological survey to establish the fact. It is perhaps very much in the same position as was the adbestos market a year or two ago. As my hon. friend knows, there was any quantity of asbestos, but the industry was almost dead. Of course the hon. member would suggest protection at once.

Any reasonable man
would.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will not get into an argument with my hon. friend about that this afternoon; we will argue it some other time. Our .business as a Manes department is to lend geological aid if necessary where prospectors have made discoveries, and to assist them in testing. But apart from the experiment made by the government in the briquetting of coal and the experiment in connection with peat, we are not trying to undertake commercial development of these ores. That is the point I am trying to make.

We are not asking the
minister to undertake commercial development. We are asking the minister to undertake the research work which he claims his department is doing, and I presume that is all he is claiming in regard to peat. Why does he not transfer his activities to questions which are pressing to-day, which are of some very considerable importance and in connection with which research work is necessary? No other question is perhaps more important than that to which I have referred. Why does the minister waste his time on matters of no importance while neglecting other matters which require attention to-day, this altogether apart from the question of protection, to which he has been good enough to refer. I am glad to know that at times he has glimmerings of intelligence in regard to the operation of his department.
I would like to ask the minister whether this is the proper place to discuss the oil well regulations?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think that had better come up under the Department of the Interior, because they are practically controlled by that department.

Before this item passes I would like to suggest to the minister that he should reduce this amount for the

Supply-Geological Survey
peat experiment. I do not see why he needs $50,000. I could tell the committee a lot about peat from my own unfortunate experience many years ago, but this is not the time to do so. I do not object to the experiment being carried on in the hope of discovering some way to utilize this natural product, but it does seem that $50,000 is too much to pay for a pure experiment. I wonder if the minister cannot reduce this vote.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have
aimed at the production of 15,000 tons of fuel this year at this plant. It is not the idea to create the impression that large commercial plants could be successfully operated because, as my hon. friend from Pictou has said, of necessity this fuel can only supply the market contiguous to the point of production. Peat cannot be shipped great distances because it is bulky and light and carries a fairly high freight rate, but this year we expect to produce 15,000 tons. We hope to produce that at $3.50 per ton, and that is about what we estimate will be the outlay during the season. We expect to recoup ourselves by the sale of peat, so we are simply asking for a sum with which to carry on this year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Geological survey, $331,000.
How many parties have you in the field this year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have
fifty-two parties.

Are there any more in
British Columbia than were there last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, there
has been a permanent arrangement with British Columbia almost since union for geological survey work. I think we have eleven parties there.

May I ask what parties
you have in Nova Scotia this year, and what districts they are in?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Mr. E. R.
Faribault is in the gold-bearing districts in Yarmouth county. He will also continue systematic geological mapping on the Annapolis quadrangle. Mr. J. A. MacDonald will make control surveys in the southwestern part of the province. Aerial photographs have been taken of this part and geological map-sheets contributory to the systematic geological and geographical survey of the province will be made from these photographs and the control surveys. Mr. I W. Jones will complete a geological survey of Springhill quadrangle. Mr. W. A. Bell will make a supplementary examination of the coal area at New Glasgow, and Mr. Bell and Mr. G. W. H. Norman will continue a systematic geological survey of Ainslie quadrangle.

I would like to ask the
minister when the reports of the work done last year will be made available?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We will
start to issue them shortly and possibly before fall all the reports having to do with the operations last year will be in your hands.
This work was done during the season of 1927, and would be completed by September of that year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, it would be later than that.

Most of the field parties in British Columbia are finished by the end of September. Could not the preliminary reports of these surveys be issued? Could not the issuance of these reports be speeded up, so that they would be available to the public at an earlier date? We will not receive those reports until July or August. Surely that could be speeded up so that the information would be made available earlier in the year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: One of our difficulties, as my hon. friend knows, is that maps must accompany these reports, and there is a good deal of work necessary to prepare the details. Possibly we could get out a summary which would be available to the public who wish to have the benefit of that information at the beginning of the spring work, but one of the difficulties here at Ottawa is that the printing bureau is working overtime on parliamentary work from the moment the session opens until it closes, and it is very difficult to get printing done.

Could we not cut down on
the sessional work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
know, but I do know that they are working nights.
Could we not cut out some of the sessional work?
I would like to refer to one other matter. Last year as the minister knows, or at all events his chief officers know, a company did a lot of deep drilling in the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A private
company?

Yes, in a search for oil.
At Governor's island near Charlottetown, P.E.I., they put down one hole to a very considerable depth; as a matter of fact I think
Supply-Mines

they put down two bore holes, but one was lost. The records of that work must be of very considerable value, and I would like to know if the department have kept in touch with the work and if they have been able to get the log of these drillings, which must contain a very considerable amount of information in regard to the strata and the possibility of oil being in that locality.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am told
that we have that log on file in the department, and it can be procured.
Similar work is now being done in Cape Breton near lake Ainslie and I presume the department is keeping in touch with the men on the ground in regard to that well?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Mines-amount required for expenses in connection with movement of coal from Alberta to Ontario and from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to Quebec and Ontario, under the provisions of orders in council P.C. 439 and P.C. 539, $150,000.

Could1 the minister give the
committee any idea of the amount of coal that will be shipped this summer?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It would
be very difficult to make even an estimate of the amount that will be moved. We know that contracts are being made for Nova Scotia coal outside of the old areas in which coal from the maritime provinces was formerly sold in Ontario; in Cochrane, for example. Bituminous coal will be sold in the territory that distance from Montreal. Alberta coal is being sold in a good many different parts of Ontario.

The minister has no idea
of the amount of coal being moved under this subsidy?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I could not
say.

When this subsidy was arranged with the Alberta government did the minister take into consideration the cost of the coal at the mine mouth? From the information I have I understand that coal of a similar character can be mined in the United States under similar conditions at about one-half the cost. I would like to know if the government has done anything to ascertain the cost of coal at the mine mouth in the province of Alberta. I understand that
[Mr. Cantley-1
the Alberta government has not been able to Obtain that cost, and I was wondering if the Dominion government have anything to show that the price charged is a fair price.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is a very difficult proposition you have presented, because so much depends on the volume and the length of time the mine is operating, to arrive at the cost of raising the coal. There is a considerable difference between the cost charged for coal in Alberta and that in the United States, but whether or not they can raise coal as cheaply, whether or not their volume is as large, and whether all the factors that go to make up the cost of coal are the same, I am unable to say.
We have not made inquiry as to the f.o.b. prices being charged, as that is a matter which the Ontario consumers or the Ontario government and the Alberta government ought to adjust between themselves. The movement is fixed at a rate o.f $6.75 per ton, and we are only interested in the freight movement of the coal; to ensure a rate which will be reasonable and just for that movement. The matter of selling coal is entirely in the hands of the two governments concerned, not in ours.

I think the federal government should be vitally concerned in the cost * of coal at the mine mouth, because, after all, if you are going to subsidize coal going to other provinces the first consideration is whether a fair price is being charged at the mine mouth. According to an inquiry which was held recently in the United States, it was shown coal was being sold at the rate of S2.25 at the mine mouth. It is evident that the operators in the United States are willing to give that cost, and I want to know why the operators in Alberta or other parts of Canada are not willing to give the same information. They have always refused to give it in Alberta, and I think the minister ought to know that there is a fixed price there. In other words, there is a ring of coal operators and they charge whatever the traffic will bear. A price of $4.50 or $4.95 at the mine mouth, in my estimation, is altogether too high. Before one cent in the way of subsidy for the moving of this coal is spent, I think it is our duty to find out whether a proper price is being charged at the mine mouth. The Alberta government and the operators have been asking this government to give certain concessions in order to obtain the Ontario market. I would like to see the Ontario market supplied with coal from the province of Alberta or from the maritime provinces,

Supply-Mines
but the operators, particularly in Alberta, have given no concessions whatsoever in order to obtain that particular market.
About ten years ago we had a similar situation in western Canada where the operators in Alberta said that if they could only obtain the Manitoba market their problems would be solved. They have now a very large share of the Manitoba market but their problems have not been solved in any way; they are just about where they were ten years ago, more mines have been opened and the mining industry is in about the same position as it was in 1918 or 1919.
The same condition applies in the United States regarding the length of time in the year the mines are operated. The mines of the United States are idle for a good period of the year, and some of them operate no longer or not even as long as do the mines in Alberta. Mr. Chairman, I do think that before' the government continues with this subsidy it should take steps to find out what it costs to produce one ton of coal in Alberta, taking all things into consideration, and then we will know whether they are worthy of consideration. At the present time prices run from $4.50 to $4.95 per ton, and when the operators of Alberta are asking the government for assistance I think they should1 find out if they are worthy of it.

How much money has been
paid in the way of subsidy, on Nova Scotia coal coming to Ontario, how much coal has been hauled under that subsidy, and where has it been shipped to in Ontario?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is in error when he states it is a subsidy; it is merely an amount that the board will fix over and above $6.75 per ton for this test movement. It is not a definite subsidy, our interest being only in the freight haul. I do not want to get the government into the position of being made responsible for coal prices either in Ontario or Alberta. That is a problem for the people who administer the Mines Act in the province of Alberta, and it is a problem for either the consumers or the government of the province of Ontario. We are only interested in the freight rate and we have agreed to assist in a test movement to demonstrate what is a fair and reasonable rate to be charged for the movement of this commodity both from the east and west. No money will be paid until the end of the season when the Board of Railway Commissioners will estimate what is reasonable and just to be paid to the railway companies for this movement, and I am asking for the $150,000 to provide against that contingency.
Is there not a subsidy being paid on Nova Scotia coal moving west?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No. There was a subsidy of one-fifth of a cent per mile up to 50 cents per ton some years ago. There was approximately $19,000 paid on that occasion for that movement. But this is the same movement as the one we inaugurated from Alberta and it is based on the same principle.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to the question of the movement of coal from the west and from Nova Scotia. As he knows, the rate from Alberta is fixed at $6.75 and from Nova Scotia points to Montreal it is is fixed at $3 and from New Brunswick at $2.10. The distance from Alberta points is practically 1,989, or say 2,000 miles. That figures out at about 3.39 mills per ton mile on which I presume the rate was based. Taking the same rate per ton mile we find that the Minto rate ought to be considerably lower than $2.10, which is the rate issued. The Canadian Pacific mileage from Minto to Montreal is 501 miles. At 3.39 mills that gives a rate of $1.70 instead of $2.10. If you take the mileage by the Canadian National road it is 547.6 miles, which would give a rate of a little qnder $1.85 instead of $2.10. Therefore by the shortest route which should govern we would be entitled to a rate of $1.70 or even by the longest route to a rate of $1.85. Why put in a rate of $2.10?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am greatly interested in this movement, but I do not think we got down to the exact figures that my hon. friend has presented. In every case in a freight movement of this kind the long haul gets the more reasonable rate. That is generally admitted. Probably my hon. friend will argue that there should not be that much difference. I am accepting his figures; I do not know the correctness of them, but I am sure he has gone into the matter fairly and that his figures are correct. We are endeavouring to treat both east and west alike in connection with this test movement. I have much more hope of assistance to the eastern industry by widening the market by the rail and water haul via Montreal than by the all-rail haul under almost any conditions.

I am not interested at
the moment in the rail and water haul. That has some advantage, I will admit. It will apply to Cape Breton; it does not apply to the mainland. The minister's statement about the long haul is all right in reference to a haul between divisional points, but it is not
Supply-M ines

a factor where the distance is 500 miles as compared with 2,000 miles where you are passing over one or several divisions to another, because your divisional charges are the same in either case.
I come to the question of the Spring Hill district where the distance is 684.4 miles, about one-third of the Alberta distance, 1 will admit, but passing over a divisional point, so that the minister's argument does not apply. The rate here should be $2.32 per ton, not $3 as we are charged for the whole province of Nova Scotia-a flat rate of $3 irrespective of distance. If you take the Stellarton district, the distance is 768 miles, and at 3.39 mills the rate would figure out at about $2.60, whereas we are charged $3. The rate from Spring Hill should of course be a little less becauses the distance is less. The rate from Sydney on the same basis would be $3.24. There I admit you are giving Sydney an advantage, but the fact is that no coal will be moved from Sydney under this scheme; it is not expected that it should be moved from there. But a large quantity of coal should be moved from Spring Hill and from the Pictou district to overcome seasonal unemployment and from those points we are asked to pay too much. A level rate for the whole province of Nova Scotia based on practically the greatest mileage that can be found in the province, namely from Sydney, and disregarding the Pictou and Cumberland fields is not fair treatment as compared with that which the other province has received in this regard. New Brunswick is entitled to a rate of $1.70 from Minto, Spring Hill a rate of $2.32 and the Pictou district a rate of $2.60. I do not think any coal will be moved from the island of Cape Breton, but it is entitled to a rate of $3. Why does the minister not give us in the several maritime coal districts the same treatment as he is giving to the west? That is the question I ask and I should like to get an answer.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The maritimes start off with an advantage of twenty per cent covering all rates. That applies in the first instance.
The 20 per cent does not apply to this special rate.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is
true, but my hon. friend is taking the total rate on the long haul against his short haul and figuring that he is working at a disadvantage. Minto coal, however, comes into
[Mr. Cantley.l
this city under the old rate. We are desirous of extending the use of it so far as we can. Minto coal has been burned in this plant.
I know that. Pictou coal comes up in the summer but not in the winter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It comes
up by rail.

No, it comes by water
to Montreal.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I did not
understand that it came by water. My understanding was that it came by rail. We are trying to give my hon. friend a rate that will put his coal into this market and that will be as nearly commensurate with the rate to the western provinces as we can make it. My. hon. friend will, I admit, find some discrepancies, but he will agree with me that when we made the attempt before, the maritime provinces were the only portion of Canada to profit by the movement. Moreover, this is a test movement. Accurate figures, I trust, will be taken of the movement. We made one zone of the province of Alberta. We do not say, for example, that the rate from Drumheller will be less than the rate from the mountains where there is perhaps a longer haul of about 200 miles. We took the maritimes as a zone and divided them into two with the exception that we gave Minto in New Brunswick, which is the shortest haul, the lowest rate.
That is not a fair statement of the facts. As regards the zoning in Alberta, the whole territory is embraced within a zone of 200 miles.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Quite right.

Nine-tenths of the coal
comes from one point, namely, Drumheller. The minister has not dealt with the maritime provinces in the same way at all. We are entitled from Minto, New Brunswick, to a rate of $1.70 on the mileage. The minister talks about a long haul and a short haul. A haul of 750 miles is by no means a short haul and it is entitled to just as equitable a rate and it costs no more per ton mile than a haul of 2,000 miles. The fact remains that we have not received fair treatment in this matter. We have been charged $3 where we ought to be charged $1.70, $2.32 and $2.60 from Minto, Spring Hill and Pictou respectively. The minister might just as well admit the situation and rectify it.

Supply-M ines

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The minister is not going to admit it at all.

I do not know that he
admits anything, but at all events he cannot change the facts, and the facts are as I have stated.
Does the hon. gentleman say that Minto coal goes to Montreal by water?

No, I was talking of
Pictou coal, which is better than Minto coal.

It was with some little surprise that I heard the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg. When he suggests that it might be wise for the sake of the industry and as a matter of research to get at the production costs of the coal, I agree with him, but when he comes along with the categorical statement that the minister and parliament should not spend one cent of this vote until after the costs of the operators have been produced, there I disagree with him, and in disagreeing with him I am in good company, because I am in his own company or that of his associates. I have in my hand a copy of an editorial from the Canadian Trade Unionist, which I would call to the hon. member's attention.
Does the hon. member know what he is quoting from when he is quoting from that paper?

I am quoting from my hon. friend's friends. It says:
The successful culmination of the negotiations that have been carried on will be a source of much gratification to all who have aided their progress. The Canadian Trade Unionist feels proud that it has taken part in the campaign. It is now four years since we published the first of our series of articles urging on Canadian workmen the value to themselves of spending the money made in Canada for the Canadian coal of a sister province.
Again:
There is still the securing of a market for the product,. . . and the influence of labour is to be seen in this resolution from the representatives of a typically working-class constituency. Like results can be obtained elsewhere.
I quote from another editorial, this time from the Labour Leader, which the hon. member for Winnipeg North may have heard of. It says:
If we take it for granted that the test is to spread over the three years movement and is an attempt to create a permanent _ Ontario market, the results as far as labour in particular is concerned are very far-reaching. They affect labour as a whole throughout the entire Dominion, not merely the trades and callings directly associated with the mining or movement of the fuel, but others as well.
In the immediate past, the condition of miners in western Canadian coal fields has been an unhappy one. Skilled workmen, they have only been able to work a little more than six months of the year.
And sometimes less than that:
Limited markets have restricted the output of the mines and made all-year-round operation an impossibility. The miners, therefore, for their off-seasons have been forced, here and there, in search of some sort of seasonal occupation.
Not only would a substantial Ontario market for the coal relieve distressing conditions among the mine workers, but it is clear that it would also stabilize labour conditions throughout the west, which are now unsettled, due to the number of men who must spend a great portion of each year looking for any sort of fill-in occupation that they can find.
As well as the direct effect on living conditions among the miners themselves and its effect on other types of business dependent on the miner's patronage, the result as far as the railways are concerned is no minor one.
It is only at that particular point that I widh to take issue with the hon. member for North Winnipeg. The miners themselves are absolutely in accord with this test movement. They feel that it has offered them some hope of greater continuity of work throughout the year, more days employment, and they leave to their own organizations the adjustment of the wage scale. But when the hon. member for North Winnipeg rises and suggests that we should not give a cent of this money until after the costs of the operators have been produced, I must disagree with him. He went further and stated categorically that the operators in Alberta had a ring and were fixing prices. I do not know where he gets his facts. I have no brief for the operators. My friendship is entirely for the miners. I have stated that often and will state it again, in front of the operators or anybody else; I am stating it now. To my knowledge there is not only no deliberate ring so far as the Drum-heller field is concerned, but there is keen competition in the securing of markets. In this city of Ottawa one of the Drumheller mines is now offering coal at a cut rate, at 25 cents a ton below the price charged by other mines. That should dispel the hon. gentleman's belief that there is any deliberate ring. That is all I wish to say on this matter at the moment, and I trust the hon. member for North Winnipeg will not be provoked any further.
Who fixes the price of Alberta coal?

The minister has told us that we must not call this a bounty. I call it
Supply-Indian Affairs

a hand-out. It is going to cost us $150,000, and surely it is worthy of a name. It must not be called a bounty or a subsidy. What would the minister call it?
