speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It would seem this might be an appropriate place to make a few observations with respect to the condition of the Eskimos. The minister has had his attention directed to this matter on more than one occasion, and considerable sums of money have been expended for the purpose of improving their condition. I understand that every winter there is considerable hardship endured by the Eskimos, and the only remedy that has been suggested1 that would be at all equal to the demands made upon the department would foe to import a number of reindeer from Norway, and to establish herds up there, as has been done so successfully by Mr. Lopp in Alaska. I know the minister gave the matter some consideration, and there is a considerable number of people who will be very anxious to know from a statement by the minister in this house just what is being done, and what may be done, in the way of affording this measure of relief to this native population of our country to whom we owe so large an obligation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The importation of reindeer was attempted by the department on the ea3t coast and was a failure, we understand, because of the fact that they were not well located on proper grazing grounds. The reindeer nearly all died. Since that time our attention has been directed to the fact that in Alaska the American government have made a very great success of the rearing and domesticating of reindeer They are rearing the reindeer in their wild state, and have a very considerable market both for the fur and the meat, and as a commercial undertaking it is proving to be quite a success. There have been in the employ of the department for two years two gentlemen who have made a study of the food and other conditions of the reindeer, and it is hoped to make a success in this direction yet. They have been in the north now for a period of two years, and we shall soon have their report. In addition to that, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), on behalf of others, approached! the department about a year ago to lease a very large territory in the vicinity of Hudson bay.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In the Mackenzie basin?
[Mr. Neill.)

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: West of Hudson bay. The land was required for individuals who had made a success of rearing reindeer in Alaska. They wished to import a very considerable herd and make a thorough test of the possibilities of raising reindeer in that territory. I think arrangements have been practically completed, and we will soon have, as a private enterprise, a herd of reindeer established there, and year by year a certain number of animals will be turned over to the government, which we will then give to Eskimos, who will be trained to establish small herds. This work we trust will' be beneficial to the Eskimos from the standpoint both of meat supply and of fur.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have no desire to detain the committee, but possibly the minister has seen a letter which was published in the Toronto Globe with respect to this matter, pointing out the conditions under which the Eskimos are living and the necessity for action being taken to provide for their wants.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is that the Rev. Mr. Walton's letter?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am referring to the letters written by him and also by Mr. R. H. Knowles of Toronto. There is also an editorial in the Globe with respect to the matter, which I placed among my files for reference when dealing with the estimates. The movement of reindeer to the Mackenzie basin will not entirely meet the demand for further consideration by the aboriginal population in another section of the northwest. There are about six thousand souls in all, and the story told of their privations and sufferings demands that action be taken to prevent a recurrence of those conditions, for the minister himself on a previous occasion pointed out that we owe to the aborigines a sacred duty that is not lightly to be disregarded. Under the circumstances, if the experiment to establish reindeer in that part of the Northwest Territories immediately concerned has been unsatisfactory, I think a larger sum should be placed at the disposal of the minister to make possible the absolute prevention of a recurrence of the hardships and suffering which those people have undergone.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am asking for a considerable sum in another place

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
-but largely for the purpose of securing supplies from the traders. The Hudson's Bay Company, for example, have posts along Coronation gulf

Supply-Indian Affairs
and around Churchill where the Eskimos congregate, and they are most likely to know whether the natives are in distress. This occurs in the winter season, when sometimes whole tribes are wiped out. I neglected to say that the investigation we are making by those two gentlemen from the United States is along Coronation gulf.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Porsild Brothers?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am not sme if that is the name. They have made a study of the subject, so we will have some assurance that there will be the necessary feed available if the deer are moved in. We are having difficulty with our Indians all through the northern territory.	On that
account we are asking for larger sums for medical attention and supplies. The high prices at which fur is selling to-day is a great incentive to the white trapper to interfere very seriously with the livelihood of the Indians-so serious that we are going to kill some of the older buffalo in the northern herd and reserve the meat for that territory.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the Globe editorial it is stated that a ninety-eight pound bag of ' flour was sold to the Eskimos at from fourteen to sixteen dollars, and a tin of beef at seventy-five cents. There are only six thousand of them in all. If that is so, I think the minister should state to the house very frankly that he regards the Dominion's obligation to feed and clothe them to be of such importance that he will see to it that the Eskimos are properly looked after. I think that is all that can be fairly asked of the department.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has brought this matter up, for it is one on which the house needs information. The reports we receive are usually from a year to eighteen months after the occurrence-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the trouble.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: -and we do not discover there has been distress and suffering until it is too late to apply a remedy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Usually they are dead.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes. So far we have had to trust pretty largely to the northern traders. We are trying to get into that territory police posts just as quickly as my hon. friend will give us the men. We have established a number of posts there during the last two or three years, and we are endeavouring to teach the natives to apply to the mounted police as our direct representatives. Let me say that I do not think those natives have always been used by the traders as they should have been, and the mounted police are exercising a very salutary influence on the traders operating in that northern territory. With the extension of the mounted police service I think we shall be able to take measures more adequately to protect the natives than we have been able to in the past.
From what I can hear in this corner you are discussing Indian affairs?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, civil government.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec, $317,107.
Will the minister explain the general increases in these votes?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In this vote there is an increase of $8,000 for relief and medical attendance. Without going into details, I may say that we have to increase our votes all along the line for assistance of this kind to our Indian wards.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is no doubt
about it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am afraid that in the future we shall have to increase these votes very materially, because we are not in any way meeting the requirements for stamping out tuberculosis, which is very prevalent amongst the Indians. Indeed, it is increasing to some extent. Of course, that means better housing, better care-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And medical attention.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes. In
every case we are asking for some increase in the votes for hospitals and so forth.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the Indian population of Canada at present?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wholly agree with
what the minister has said. There is evidence on many reserves that notwithstanding the efforts made the population is decreasing, and if there is any duty we owe in the world it is the duty we owe the Indians and Eskimos, the aborigines who are the wards of the nation. I should like the minister to make it perfectly clear that early this year he will take steps to prevent destitution and starvation among the Indians and Eskimo population in the far northern part of the country. If we do not move now these people will die of starvation this winter.
Supply-Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the Coronation gulf area "we now have a mounted police force which was recently established on Baffin island. In the north, where the Indians congregate, we are also policed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But further east?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The northern end of Quebec is the one weak spot in the organization.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And that is where the
Eskimos are suffering.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a
considerable number of Eskimos there and we have some apprehension, but we are taking the precaution to ensure that the traders will at least endeavour to see that no destitution occurs. But we moist have a police force there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And start now.
What is the acreage in Indian reserves in each of the provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I can give
the number of reserves but I doubt whether I can give the exact acreage.
Have certain lands, formerly Indian reservations, been acquired or taken over by the government, and if so, what lands were given in substitution therefor?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I can best
answer that question by citing what is going on at present in the Peace river country where there are three small reserves in the thickly settled district there. There are not very many Indians on them, it is true, but what we propose doing there, subject always of course to approval by the Indian band themselves, is to sell these and substitute other lands which are not so valuable and which are of a greater distance westward. Generally speaking, where there is a sale of a reserve or of any portion of a reserve, the sale takes place after a vote has been taken by the Indian band on the reserve. Their consent is obtained and the land is then sold at public auction. That method was departed from in some cases when soldier settlement was quite active. The Saddle lake reserve in Alberta is one I know of particularly. In that case there was set aside at a fixed value a certain portion of the reserve, with the consent of the Indians, of course, and $10 an acre was decided upon as the price. There was no public auction in that instance. But in the case of the Blackfoot reserve where the land was not required-it is in the vicinity of my hon. friend's constituency-the Indians voted and

the land was sold at public auction to the highest bidder. The practice in all cases is, first, to obtain the consent of the band, and secondly, to sell at public auction to the highest bidder, the funds to be preserved of course in the interests of the band itself.

Why was
that procedure departed from in the case of the Saddle lake reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It had been presumed that the land was required for soldier settlement purposes, but it finally turned out that it was not; and as the government were in duty bound to pay over the $10 an acre to the Indians or to the band funds other disposition had to be made of the land.
What was that disposition?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Part of it
was sold to British families. I know there was one portion that went to local people by allotment at $10 an acre-a small portion on the eastern side of the reserve.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was not sold by auction?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does not the law require it to be sold by auction?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It was 6old to the Soldier Settlement Board. It had gone out of the control of the Department of Indian Affairs, and it was sold* to th>
board who made this adjustment.

Was not a
large block of that Saddle lake reserve disposed of to one corporation or organization, and by them resold, they being in full control?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is referring to -the British families settled under the Hebridean association. They were settled by the Soldier Settlement Board on these lands which were assumed to be required for soldier settlers but were not, and which were subsequently settled by these Hebrideans.

I did not
suppose that the Hebrideans, who were brought out under the Scottish Immigration Aid Association, had settled there at all.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The minister (Mr. Forke) now tells me that thjey were not; they were British settlers who were put on the land under the British Empire settlement scheme.

Supply-Indian Affairs

Then no
large portion of the reserve was disposed of en bloc to any organization or association?
No; only in so far as the Soldier Settlement Board acquired it at $10 an acre.
Was 110 an acre the average price of raw land around the Saddle lake reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I cannot
say; I should think so.

Perhaps the Minister of
Immigration can tell us.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It happened prior to our time; the allotment was made under the previous government. But $10 an acre was a fair price for raw land in that vicinity at that time.

What reserves in the
Peace river country have been voted on by Indians?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: None as yet.
Was a vote taken last summer?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No; an attempt was made but we did not get the Indians together.

Is it .the intention to
take a vote again?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This summer.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indians-Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, $918,257.
Will the minister explain the ramifications of this vote? It is a large vote and there is an increase.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The largest proportion of the vote, $40,000, is for destitute Indians, to meet treaty obligations. The three prairie provinces cover a very considerable area and we require this additional amount. I emphasize -the necessity for doing something, along with the provincial government, to provide hunting grounds for the Indians apart from the reserves on which they live. If we cannot succeed in doing that, and the Indians come into competition with the white man and are obliged to earn their livelihood, they will starve to death. That is as the situation appears to us. Consequently we are constantly asked for more money to relieve destitution and for illness resulting from destitution, and we have pared these sums to
the lowest possible amount. These Indians are our wards; we must do the best we can for them, and without going into a detailed explanation I would say to my hon. friend . that every dollar of this amount will be needed for the purpose for which it is voted.

In regard to the
policy of the department I should like to ask the minister whether it is contemplated that the Indians will have to earn their living by hunting, and if so, whether it is a good thing to bring young Indians to boarding schools, keep them there for six or eight years, then turn them out again without having given them the opportunity to acquire hunting habits.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have given this question very considerable attention and I have watched the development of some of these young people, so I might say that I have very great hopes of making a change in connection with the young Indians whom we can put at once into the occupation of farming. For example, take the Blood reserve in Alberta; we have an allocation of land for the young student as soon as he is ready to leave school, and we endeavour to build a small house for him and to become responsible for the purchase of stock and implements, although in a very limited way. We have every prospect of success there, and the reason I lay so mudh emphasis on this is because I am led to believe it will be successful through what I have seen on the Six Nations reserve in Ontario. Of course there are good and bad Indians just as there are good and bad white men, but on that reserve they are making a fair success of agriculture. However, in answer to my hon. friend's direct question about the hunting Indian, the northern Indian, wfho is brought to school and then turned loose at the age of fifteen or sixteen years, neither a hunter nor a half-trained white man; that is the problem which is giving us the most concern at the present time. The Indians who live in agricultural areas usually work for the surrounding farmers, and they make good workmen. I am not decrying the advantages of education to the young Indian, but we should have something to put him at as soon as he leaves school in order that he may earn his livelihood, and we have not overcome that difficulty as yet, although we are giving it very careful consideration.

Just one other
question in connection with these industrial schools. Would it not be well to encourage

Supply-Indian Affairs

the young Indians to become Canadian citizens, or to make it possible for them to become Canadian citizens, in order that they might assume the full responsibilities of citizenship?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Of course
that is the whole idea behind the education given them, and it is the solution of the whole difficulty. However, When that happy condition will be attained is a different matter. I do think that the quicker we teach them the virtuous ways of the white man and his methods of earning a livelihood the better it will be for our Indian wards and the sooner they will be able to assume the white man's responsibility. That is what we have in view.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think perhaps the
minister might have presented the other side of the picture as well. There is no doubt that in some parts of western Canada the Indians have produced- very substantial quantities of grain. In Saskatchewan, say south of the Saskatchewan river; in Alberta, say south of Strathcona, and in Manitoba, they have produced very substantial quantities of grain. Perhaps the minister has the information with him, and I am sure the committee would be interested to know the number of bushels of grain produced by the Indians in those provinces last year. I visited two of the reserves last year and was greatly taken with the improved conditions under which they are carrying on agriculture. I am not an authority upon agriculture at all, but the amount of grain they produced was really very wonderful. At one place, as the minister will recall, they had an elevator which was subsequently sold; they had many thousands of bushels of grain which they sold during the year; they had good horses, some excellent cattle and good equipment. In some instances very active government supporters were anxious to sell them increased quantities of equipment to an extent far in excess of their requirements; no doubt the minister will recollect that in one case so much of this machinery was sold that if they had produced enough grain to utilize the number of harvesting machines in their possession they might have ranked with the great grain producers of the world. However, that condition was overcome in due season, like most things of the world; we will get them in due season if we faint not. I think the committee might be interested in hearing just what these Indians 
produced last year; I think the result is highly creditable to those who have had the responsibility of conducting the business of the Indian department in its various ramifications.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I want to
make it clear that only a small proportion of our Indian population earn their livelihood through agriculture; if all Indians did so our difficulties would be ended. I am not pleading for the Indian capable of earning his livelihood in agriculture but I am pleading very strongly for the Indian, wherever he may be, in whatever province of Canada, who is not engaged in agriculture and who is having rather a difficult time. However, as my hon. friend has pointed out, I think it would be of interest to the committee to know just how the Indians have come out in the production of grain. Last year in the three prairie provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta they had 37,307 acres of land under crop which produced 603,621 bushels of wheat; of oats they had about 21,000 acres under cultivation, which produced about 398,000 bushels; of barley they had 4,441 acres under cultivation, which produced 75,435 bushels. Then we have a very detailed statement of the amount of vegetables they raised, the hay and so on; I think the figures I have given will suffice, but if the committee desire I will give a copy to Hansard and have the complete statement put in.

What seems to be the
chief difficulty in getting a vote taken among the Indians in regard to the disposal of some of the reserves, such as those in the settled parts of the Peace River country?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Well, as my hon. friend knows, it is very difficult to get those Indians on the reserve, and he also knows that unless we get a fairly representative vote we are likely to have trouble with the band because they were not consulted. That happens on almost every occasion, but we are making a determined effort to have that vote taken this year, and I hope the vote will represent the great majority ^of the band interested.
Is it necessary that the Indians meet on the reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

Is it not possible to take the vote when they come to get their treaty money?

Supply-Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, we have followed the principle of having the votes taken on the reserve. I had exactly the same difficulty on a small reserve west of Edmonton, where we tried for three years to get a vote taken. Last year we finally succeeded.

One of the great troubles in connection with these reserves in the Peace River country occurs in grasshopper years. Although the neighbouring farmers do their best to cope with the plague, the reserve close by seem to contain a plentiful supply of grasshoppers for the whole community. That fact has stirred up a tremendous amount of feeling in the community.

I have just one remark to
make in connection with this item. I should like to ask the minister to give us an assurance that the young Indians after they leave these industrial schools will be given the necessary equipment with which to start farming on the reserves. I have had a good many complaints from the Indians to the effect that they have had difficulty in getting the department to give them equipment. I do not suggest that there is ground for all these complaints, but I would like to have the assurance of the minister that he will be as liberal as possible in the furnishing of equipment to these young Indians who are willing to start farms of their own.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I think I
can give my hon. friend that assurance, but I would not promise that we will satisfy the young Indians, because they want a full set of equipment to start with. We try to be as generous as we can in starting up a young man in that way, and I do not think there is any complaint to be made.

Do these Indians receive
agricultural education at the school?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

How much land is there in
connection with the school at Edmonton?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think the farm consists of about eight hundred acres.
Does the young Indian have to pay for the equipment out of the proceeds of the crops, or is it given to him?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We expect
him to pay for it. He does not always do so, but we lead him to understand that he is under an obligation to repay us.
Is this equipment charged at full price, or at the cost price plus a certain percentage of profit?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the case of animals, we have to purchase them at the going price, and the Indian is charged exactly what we pay for them. We can make a very advantageous arrangement regarding implements, because we are buying for about a dozen reservations. We get the advantage of a discount, which is given to the Indians.

Is the
department contemplating doing anything regarding the debts some of these Indians have incurred? I should like the minister to state whether some of this vote is for that purpose, or whether there is any provision made for that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have
investigated all these accounts, and where receipts can be produced from the Indian agent we feel theie is an obligation on the department to pay. Unfortunately there were a lot of transactions where the agent was never consulted, a sale direct to the Indian. We have made no attempt to clean these up, but year by year we have been wiping off all these old accounts where receipts could be produced. We have not been using any of these votes for that purpose, but have endeavoured to do this by using the band funds and other means. I would like to say that we have them all cleared up, but there was a very considerable amount when I started in to fix up this mess.

Do I
understand from the minister that there has never been a vote for this purpose?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am informed that we have never had a vote for this purpose.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indians-Yukon, $19,000.

How many Indians are
there in the Yukon territory?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
stagedirection

Indians-general, $231,500.

Would the minister tell the
committee the total Indian population of Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100,000.

Supply-Indian Affairs

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Indian education, including the construction of school buildings, $2,160,310.

Would the
minister be good enough to give us a general statement in regard to this item of Indian education and how it is carried on?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
With the
exception of the day schools, this work is carried on very largely by the religious organizations-such churches as the Roman Catholic, the Anglican, the United church and the Presbyterian. In the day schools all the teachers are employed by the government. They must be certificated, and they are inspected by the provincial school inspectors of the province in which they are located. Under the old system the churches asumed the whole responsibility regarding the boarding schools, and received a per capita grant for this work from the government. When I came here I changed the system somewhat, as I found most of the church organizations were in rather severe financial difficulties. We took over such buildings as we deemed to be decent and worth while repairing, and commenced a program of construction of new buildings. We have been spending in the neighbourhood of $500,000 or $550,000 annually in the purchase and construction of new buildings, keeping in mind the necessities of the organizations which have this work in hand, and the necessities of the communities in which they are built. In the British Columbia vote there is an additional $100,000, due to a recommendation made by the joint committee which dealt with this matter last year.
I wanted to get a comparison of the Indians educated in the day schools and in the so-called private schools.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We are constructing a new boarding school at Shuben-acadie, Nova Scotia. We believe better training can be given the Indian child in the boarding school than in the day school, because it is very difficult to get him to be at all regular in his attendance at the day school. We have him under control all the time in the boarding school, as he remains there during the whole school period. In the day schools, which are located in all the provinces, we have 4,005 boys and 3,850 girls, or a total of 7,864. In our residential schools, which are located in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the Northwest Territories, 'British Columbia and the Yukon, we have 3,208 boys, 3,433 girls, or a total of 6,641. Therefore there are all told about 14,000 children attending school.

In the Indian schools, particularly the boarding schools, does the department supervise or control in any way the program, for instance, of technical and agricultural work? Is there a defined system whereby the young Indian, instead of receiving the ordinary education which is of little value to him, really becomes a productive agent? I ask the question because I know from my experience in visiting the Indian schools that there is a great waste. In other words, they reach a certain stage; they learn to read and write and a few other things, and then they have absolutely nothing to fall back upon. Is there a defined program of technical education of the Indian boys?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The very difficulty that my hon. friend mentions is one to which we have given some thought in an endeavour to see if we can remedy it; but if he knows anything about the Indian, his habits and environment, he will1 realize the difficulty. We are endeavouring to teach the girls domestic work in addition to the ordinary public school curriculum, and the boys, such outdoor work as will come to hand in any given institution. In Kamloops, for example, the boys are trained in irrigation work because in that territory the boys are going out into fruit growing areas and drier sections. In the north we give them as much education as we can in regard to agriculture, even as labourers, if need be, so that when they go out they may carry on in competition with their white brothers.
Have there been any epidemics amongst the Indians apart from the tubercular trouble?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, what the doctors call the "flu" or influenza is a very serious menace to the Indians in the wooded areas, but we have not had any serious outbreak recently. Tuberculosis is the worst enemy we have to contend with amongst the Indian tribes.

Supply-Interior-N.W.T.
Would the minister give the committee some information as to the number of buffalo taken from Wainwright park to the north?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: For three years we have been transferring young buffalo under two years of age from Wainwright park to the territory in the north. We started this as an experiment, but we now have a very considerable herd in the north and I doubt if we shall continue it after this year. We are sending up another contingent of buffalo this year. We feel that from this point onward the surplus stock both at Wainwright and at La.mont might very well be slaughtered and the hides sold, the government getting the advantage of the sale of the meat and the fur.
Has the minister any report on how the buffalo are doing in the north?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They are doing very well. They have mixed with the native herd there. True, the buffalo that are in captivity are not as large as the northern buffalo, but there is no doubt that they will be a very fine herd if they are protected.
I have had some complaints regarding the refusal by the department to parties seeking licenses to buy fur in the Northwest Territories. What are the conditions in regard to that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The act of
last year was to have come into effect this year. Of course I am very anxious that we should receive some revenue out of the Northwest Territories, and we are entitled tc get it, particularly as all the other provinces in Canada have a fur tax; but through a mistake in the revision of the statutes by the committee the wrong year was inserted, which would have meant that I would have to reintroduce the act at this session to have the matter rectified. I thought it well to let it go and it will come into effect next year automatically under the provisions of the act. My reason for doing this was that I received a very largely signed petition from the residents of the Northwest Territories protesting against the imposition of this tax and asking that some investigation be had with respect to the administration of affairs up there as they affect the Indians, and the white people as well, living along the Mackenzie basin. Three weeks ago I sent a representative of the Department of the Interior and a representative of the Department of Indian Affairs up there. We have
given them a list of questionnaires and they are to meet the people, at convenient points which will be well advertised to the residents of the north, to take evidence not only with respect to the fur tax, but with regard to every other matter that may be agitating the minds of the residents of that territory, and to report back to the government this fall. But the act will come into effect automatically in 1929.
On what grounds were certain parties refused licenses to go into the Northwest Territories to trade?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No one is refused a license who will settle down at one point. If he will designate the place where he wishes to trade, we issue the license at once, but the difficulty is that we have had so many people in the past who are known as transient traders Our Assyrian friends are very fond of that kind of thing. As my hon. friend knows, the custom in the past among the legitimate traders has been for them to make loans either by way of supplies or of money to the trappers, who then go out and get a supply of fur and bring it back and pay their debts by .the sale of that fur. But the difficulty is that along may come one of these chaps who sometimes pays cash, and who travels daily and picks up the fur that rightly belongs to the individual who has grubstaked the trapper or lent him the money, and then the travelling trader disappears out of the country. We found this was an evil which we had to take some steps to remedy, and our remedy was to give everyone a license who will settle down and trade at any given point. We want to know where they are going to trade, and we issue a lioense1 bo them for that particular locality. They cannot go in and settle down at any designated point without opening what we know as a post. The man we have prohibited from trading is the trapper who travels around and picks up the fur, and usually cheats the man from whom he buys it.
Are any of the buffalo herd in captivity?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: None of the herd is in captivity in the sense that we have a fence around them, but we have wardens looking after them. They are in the same position as that formerly occupied by a herd of cattle.

Has it been found necessary to take any steps to nrotect them from wolves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Does my
faon. friend mean the young buffalo? No. They mix with the herd, which will defend them against the attacks of the wolves. The wolves always pull down the older and weaker buffalo, and it would be pretty dangerous for the calves if they were not protected from the wolves by the other members of the herd. Our losses from wolves in the past were not serious, but we are carrying on an open warfare against them. We pay a very high bounty for the skin, and encourage the hunting of the wolf as much as possible.
How much is the bounty?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Thirty dollars.

Under this vote
there is investigational work carried on. What does that consist of?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The investigation is very largely investigation of the territory. For example, we have men who are investigating pastures for the reindeer. We have investigations of various matters going on there. There is the investigation, for instance, by these men who were sent up to hear the grievances and bring back reports.

The Minister of the Interior in February last contributed an article t<o the Natural Resources of Canada magazine which challenged at least my admiration. He said in part:
The great expansion of the pulp and paper industry indicated above is cause for concern as to the adequacy of pulpwood supplies to meet the future demands of the industry. It is my opinion that gross production has been developed as far as it should be, for the time being at least. Until we are more certain that our pulpwood supplies will sustain the industry on a permanent basis there is no justification for continuation of the rather hectic expansion witnessed in the past few years. Rather the time is more opportune for concentration of effort upon refinement of methods and the more complete manufacture at Canadian mills of pulpwood extracted from Canadian forests.
I wish the minister would implement these ideas with action with respect to the pulpwood situation in Canada, Last year Mr. Angus Graham, of the Quebec Forestry Association, in an address that he delivered at Tacoma on the Pacific coast, threw a little light on this subject by saying that in the province of Quebec there were 110,000 square mile's of pulpwood limits, and the pulpwood averaged 6.4 cords per acre. Last year we exported from Canada 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood. That represented an area of 360 square miles denuded of pulpwood timber, to be sent across the line to enhance the prestige and prosperity of the United States. It would seem to me that this is a serious state of affairs. We 'sent 1,500,000 cords of pulpwood across the line when we should have manufactured it here in our own country. We received for it $15,000,000. If that 1,500,000 cords had been manufactured into paper in Canada at $65 a ton, it would have produced $80,000,000 worth of paper. Deducting the $15,000,000 that we received for this 1,500,000 cords from the $80,000,000 that we would have received had we manufactured it into paper,

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
we have a loss of $65,000,000 to this country. If we had unlimited quantities of pulpwood the situation would be different, but as it is we can see the end of our supply. The Minister of the Interior sees the end of it and why is now not the time to put an export tax on pulpwood and let it go to the mills in our own country to be manufactured into paper here, giving employment to labour and tending to the enrichment of Canada generally?
1.500.000	cords of pulpwood, if manufactured in this country, would mean a population of
250.000	more for Canada. We are bribing people to come to this country to go on the land, to go here, there and everywhere. Why not induce them to come here by building up our industries and offering them opportunities? There is not one argument against preventing the exportation of spruce pulpwood. There may be some slight argument in favour of allowing poplar pulpwood to be sent across the line because there is hardly the demand for poplar here that we would like to see. It is a tree that grows rapidly and dies quickly. It may be all right to export poplar pulpwood across the line, until we develop the soda pulp process to a greater extend in this country. Economists tell us that it costs at least $25 a cord to raise spruce pulpwood timber here, and we are letting it go out of this country at $10 a cord. Let us look a little further into the future, and make this a country to which people will be attracted without the extraordinary inducements we have been offering them in the past.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is a
matter that has been raised almost yearly. The department have been giving the question of an export tax some consideration, and I confess that to me it appeals very strongly. But this is one of the difficulties. Immediately, it is a tax that will be borne by the Canadian who sells the wood; he will have to accept a reduced price. In the maritimes and in Quebec I am told that the competition due to the wood going out of the country has the effect of raising the price for the pulpwood manufactured in Canada. There may not be a very great deal in that argument, but it has been presented to me. May I say why I am so much interested in this? If the present quantity of wood exported continued, the revenue from an export tax of 50 cents to $1 a cord would enable us to extend our fire protection activities to a much larger degree without calling upon the treasury for any money. The objection raised when this matter has been discussed is that a large proportion of the pulpwood, particularly from
the east, is under contract to American concerns. They have been coming into Canada and establishing plants at a pretty rapid rate during the last year or two. As to overproduction, we have reached that stage now, and I may point out to my hon. friend that beyond placing an export tax on our wood we have very little control over the provincial forests, other than those in the three prairie provinces and in the railway belt in British Columbia. But in Manitoba, where a very considerable export was going on, we now have established a mill and we do control the territory from which the operators get their supplies of pulpwood. I have made the deal contingent on those people purchasing nearly all the wood offered by the farmers and those who have private limits. I propose this year to have a survey of the cutting going on in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and next year I shall try to limit the extent of those operations. I know some of my friends from Manitoba will not like to hear this, because many of the farmers in the northern district earn their livelihood by cutting and selling pulpwood, and most of it goes over into the United States. Now we are keeping the bulk of it in Canada, and it will be manufactured at the Pine Falls mill in Manitoba. I do not think they will require to manufacture a single stick of pulpwood cut off their own limit; all will be purchased from settlers in the locality. That is what we have done where we control the situation. I am in hopes that our action will be followed by the provinces in dealing with this matter.

Already British Columbia,
Ontario and Quebec prohibit the exportation of timber except from privately owned lands. That is why I am asking the government to impose an export tax. This parliament is the only body with power to do so. I do not care for an embargo; I think an export tax should be levied. We have just passed the apex of the lumber industry, and from now on it will begin to decline. I have seen the forests wiped out in several states of the union, and I realize the seriousness of our own position. When we lose our forest wealth we are losing one of our greatest assets. It is all nonsense to talk of the yearly increment keeping pace with the yearly cut. It was said the other day ihat in Anticosti the annual growth would keep pace with the cutting of the timber. That is arrant nonsense to all who know anything about forest conditions. Let any hon. gentleman the next time he goes to Hull count the annular rings

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
on the pulpwood piled along the street at the boundary, and he will find that thirty-five, forty and fifty years is the age of those trees. Our spruce pulpwood is the best we have. Let us conserve it. Spend money ad lib to protect it, if possible, from insect pests and fire. But Jet us stop exportation, which is economically foolish. It can be done, sir, and now is the time.

Does the tree-planting
forestry stations vote come under this item?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It comes under protection of timber, but my hon. friend may as well proceed.

Since the forestry station at Indian Head is near my home I have gathered some information which I should like to present to the committee. The Indian Head treeplanting station was established1 in 1904. Another was established at Sutherland, Saskatchewan, in 1914. The purpose of these stations is the propagation and distribution of seedlings and cuttings for the formation of wind1-breaks; permanent plantations for forestry research; demonstration of fruit-growing and horticultural possibilities under tree protection. The early distribution of seedlings and cuttings to bona fide farmers has increased rapidly, from 58,800 to 47 farmers in 1904, to over
5,000,000 annually to between 5,500 and 6,000 farmers. Up to the spring of 1927, 93,000,000 broad leaf seedlings and cuttings and 2,568,000 evergreen seedlings and transplants have been distributed for prairie planting. This represents the establishment of between 45,000 and 50,000 windbreaks and shelter belts in the three prairie provinces. Observations are madte annually by tree-planting inspectors of thousands of plantations. In this way the service maintains a close check on the success of the distribution scheme. In 1921, 7,643 plantations were observed, and 6,292, or 83 per cent, were found to be in a good healthy condition; 1,331, or 14 per cent, were classed as in fair shape, and likely to respond to better treatment. In 1001 there were only 54 farmers requesting assistance in tree-planting. 1927 was a banner year in prairie tree-planting. 12.528 farms were listed for inspection either for further tree-planting or for new plantations. Indications point to a heavier demand in 1928. The appropriation for tree-planting in 1910 was $29,592. At the time the distribution averaged not more than 2,500,000 trees, and instruction service was given to 6,718 farmers. In 1926 the appropriation necessary to carry on the work had increased to $79,000. but close to 7,000,000 trees were being distributed, and inspection and transplanting services were 
being given to over 12,500 farmers. The estimate for 1928-29 is over $94,000, an increase of about 16 per cent. There are now 40,000 plantations, and these valued at $300 each would represent $12,000,000, or, $11,200,000 in excess of the total cost since 1.901. That gives in a concise form something of the work that is being done. For every dollar expended at this station the country is getting a full dollars' worth in return. The work is excellently supervised, and is carried on in a way which is likely to bring continued success such as has been achieved in the past. It is only fair that I should take this opportunity to express this appreciation of the work that is being done there.

I wish to refer to the regulations in regard to the control of natural gas.
I have here a clipping from the Calgary

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
Herald from which I learn that a gentleman named Davies, who is said to be an expert on this subject, states that:
Gas equivalent to 87J carloads of coal is being wasted at Turner valley daily, and 140,000 horse-power are being burned up daily as a result of gas wastage from wells now under production.
He states that the total gas production in Turner valley at the present time is estimated to be 91,500,000 cubic feet per day. Further on this statement is made:
Taking the figures of 22,000,000 as being the total average used each day, at present there are 91,000,000 less 22.000,000 or 69,000,000 cubic feet being burned each day. During the coldest winter days this amount would drop to
58,000,000, but in the warm summer days it
would rise to 81,000,000	Then, 20,000
cubic feet of Turner valley gas under average temperature and pressure in Calgary equals approximately one ton of good Drumheller coal. Then, 20,000,000 cubic feet of natural gas equals 1,000 tons of coal and 70,000,000 cubic feet of gas equals 3,500, tons of coal. There are forty tons to a car; therefore this means eighty-seven and a half cars of coal being wasted each day.
I will not quote further from this article but I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that, according to this authority, we are wasting three times as much gas as we are using in the Turner valley field. That means that if we have a sufficient supply of gas to last Calgary and other towns sixty years, we are going to use it up in twenty 3rears and people will then have to go back to coal. Natural gas or even its equal * i3 something which it is almost impossible for us to produce once we have wasted it, and we shall have to go back to coal. There are many places in Ontario and the United States where natural gas has been wasted, and now that the fields are exhausted the people have had to resort to burning coal at a greater cost and certainly at greater inconvenience. Natural gas is possibly the best fuel for cooking and heating which we have, although of course it would not be difficult to get the hon. member for Bow River to except Alberta coal. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I find in the regulations, as printed and distributed by the department, the following under regulation 29:
In case natural gas is discovered through boring operations on a location, the lessee shall take all reasonable and proper precautions to prevent the waste of such natural gas, and his operations shall be so conducted as to enable him, immediately upon discovery, to control and prevent the escape of such gas.
Is the minister enforcing that regulation? Most of these wells are drilled on Dominion government land and I am sure he will realize
that something should be done. I ask him now whether he is taking steps to enforce the regulations; if not perhaps he would enlighten the committee as to the reason for not doing so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The matter is one to which we have been giving a great deal of attention in our department, because the waste of natural gas is rather serious. We have tried to study the question and the results of our investigation would indicate that we cannot shut off that gas. The difficulty of holding the piping, under the most tremendous pressure which we encountered in the first wells, has been overcome by the cementing of the pipe into the limestone rock before drilling into the parent body itself. I had thought of reinforcing the piping from that point upward so that we might be able to hold the pressure. But after we had investigated that scheme to some extent we discovered that with any volume of flow through the four and a half inch pipe, you cannot make it a profitable undertaking for the extracting of the gasoline content, so that to that extent the well would be useless. We had therefore to abandon that idea. The thing that interested me most happened about three weeks ago. A gentleman said that if he got the assurance that he would have no difficulty in procuring gas and delivering it, he would undertake to organize a company to lay a pipeline as far as Winnipeg, piping this gas to Winnipeg and intervening towns and hamlets, and using it to that extent. As my hon. friend knows, there has been a very decided aversion to the exportation of gas; for about three years attempts have been made to secure permission to export gas from a well near the international boundary, and no one felt like taking the responsibility of permitting the export of that gas. Of course in that case it is not escaping, but if the oil industry in the Turner valley is to go on we must make provision for free flowage from the parent supply or it cannot be profitably taken off. We have proven that, and some method must be found to take care of the extra amount of gas which cannot be utilized for the purposes for which they are now using it. We have thought of lampblack, but as my hon. friend knows that article is so cheap that it is hardly worth while making the venture, and in addition it is a very expensive way of using the gas. However, I wish to assure my hon. friend that the Alberta government have become interested in this question and they propose to study it. I have been in communication with them and have offered such information as we have gathered, and in conjunction with them we are putting our men to
3834	COMMONS
Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
work to see if something cannot be done to utilize this escaping gas, which I agree should be curtailed and stopped as nearly as it is possible to do so without injuring the industry itself, because I think my hon. friend will agree that the industry is rather valuable. I may be frank in saying that I have thought that in connection with the territory we control we should discourage the sinking of any more wells until some method has been worked out for the utilization of this surplus product.

I am glad to hear the minister say that he would like to stop the wastage of this gas, because this is really a very serious question. According to the estimates which I read, an amount of gas equal to about 3,400 tons of coal is being burned up every day.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There was
one thing I forgot to mention. About 60 per cent of the present volume of production is not under the control of the federal government; it comes from privately owned property.

It seems to me that the government might very well go so far as to exercise control over that property also; I do not think that would be going beyond the powers which we should exercise. Let me bring to the attention of the committee and the minister section 29a of the regulations:
In the event of natural gas being discovered through boring operations conducted on a petroleum and natural gas location acquired under the provisions of the regulations-if the escape of such gas is not prevented-the minister may take such effective means as may appear to him to be necessary or expedient in the public interest to control and prevent the escape of the natural gas-[DOT]
It seems to me that those words are very clear; if it is in the public interest to prevent this waste the minister has the power to step in and take any measures which may be necessary to that end. Personally I think the minister might go the limit in preventing this waste, and I also think that if he has no effective way of preventing the waste of gas from the wells already drilled certainly he should discourage the drilling of any more wells until such time as he is willing or able to take measures to prevent this waste. It may be going quite a long way to suggest that we prevent the drilling of these wells, but I think this is one of our most valuable natural resources, and in the exploitation of our resources there is nothing I dislike more than to see that gas burning away every day. There is such a volume of gas burned that at night the reflection of the fire can be seen for a distance of fifty miles. It is quite a sight, and

is worth going a long distance to see, but every time I see it I am impressed with the way we are wasting our natural resources. It is a shame; I do not know any other word for it. I do not want to lay all the blame on the minister; possibly he finds himself in a difficult situation, but if he would enforce the regulations which I read and which were in force when the leases were granted I think he could stop the waste. The last regulation which I read gives him power to act in the matter, and as far as I am concerned I would go a long wiay in supporting him if he would stop the waste of the gas.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
While we
might make all the regulations in the world we could apply them only where we have jurisdiction, and we have not jurisdiction over privately owned lands in Alberta. I am not seeking to escape in that way; I do not want my hon. friend to think I am looking for a way out, but two difficulties are created. One difficulty is that the same field of gas which is under the privately owned lands is also under the lands controlled by the Dominion, upon which we issue leases. That land we can control, but if we shut down our people immediately they would have a complaint beoause the people on the other land could continue. That difficulty can be overcome only by co-operation between the two governments. My hjon. friend knows the value of that industry; if we shut it off at once and stop the individuals or companies who have spent large sums of money to develop that field we would face a great deal of contentious criticism. However, I am thoroughly alive to the wastage which is going on and no one deplores it more than I do. I would hesitate very seriously before issuing a lease which would permit more wells to be sunk on Dominion lands until we find at least some partial remedy for this waste.

Is it not true that a number of wells have been started on Dominion lands within the last year? We had this question up last session, and I know the minister then admitted the importance of the matter. If these wells were allowed to be drilled last year and we do not take any steps now, probably a number of additional wells will be drilled this year and it will be all the more difficult to stop it. This has been going on now for two years; it is getting greater all the time and that is why I am taking the time of the committee to try and interest them in the matter. I think

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
parliament would not be going too far if we put privately owned lands under the same regulation, provided we have power to do so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We cannot do that.

I do not think we should
allow any person to waste such a valuable resource, and personally I do not think we would be going too far if we took that action.

I understand that a man by the name of McClymont was engaged as an accountant in the Department of the Interior. A report was made in due course and signed by the. deputy minister of the department, but I understand no action was taken regarding it. The compiler of the report at a later date threatened through the press to make certain statements with regard to what had been going on in the department, and I believe an order in council was passed appointing a special commission to look into the charges, or, as the minister says, the so-called charges. This commission was composed of one man, a Mr. Smith, who unfortunately has been known in Ottawa for a number of years as a very strong partisan. This commission sat in camera, or what I would call double camera, because certain information which was requested to be taken down was not taken down at all. I should like to know why he has not been punished if

that he read it all, and that he also read the evidence. That is the information I have. If I am wrong, my hon. friend is quite at liberty to say so. My hon. friends have also put on the order paper certain requests for information with respect to the sale of school lands. It is a fact, is it not, that we have them on the order paper?

I neglected to file the complete files in connection with those matters. He asked this man, on half a dozen occasions, as the evidence will disclose, if that was all the evidence he had to offer, and according to the evidence he said that he was through; that every statement he had to make had been presented and was embodied in the report. I do not wish to make with respect to this individual statements that would reflect in any way upon him, but anyone who has read the statements in the newspapers-and I have been bombarded with them now for nearly two years and I have never yet met this individual-will consider them a sufficient answer in themselves, without going much further into them. Refund Case 1
Ethel Truscott, widow, Battleford - $100 refund due her re overpayment made-sale 1060-file 31458.
This relates to the sale of the southeast quarter of section 11, township 50, range 2, west of the 4th meridian, which land was sold at Llo.vdminster on the 23rd June, 1909, to Mr. Alex Gordon at the rate of $10 per acre, and was assigned in April, 1911, to Mr. George C. Hodson.	.
In July, 1912, Mr. L. H. Truscott paid into the department $72 on account of accrued interest and under date of the 19th July, 1912, a receipt for the money was sent to Mr. Truscott. and he was advised that said receipt was made out in the name of Mr. George C. Hod-son. the recorded holder, and further that if he had acquired the interest of said George C. Hodson it would be necessary to file an unconditional assignment from Mr. Hodson to himself and have same registered in the department in order that the land might be recorded in his name and the department recognize him as the recorded holder.

Livingston and Atkinson who were acting on behalf of the representatives of the estate of the late Mr. Truscott advised the department that the widow was left in poor circumstances with a small family and that they thought it only fair that she be not required to pay any penalty such as an increased rate of interest, as provided for in the amendment to the Dominion Lands Act of 1918.

On the 28th June, 1920, Plater remitted a draft for the sum of $2,116.89, as payment in full. This amount, however, when applied as short $2.03, which was afterwards remitted by Plater, and patent issued in his favour bearing date of the 25th August, 1920.

That is statutory and we have no control over it. That is the explanation in regard to the claim that we have retained out of that sale $100 which are not entitled to retain. John Gair, farmer, Killam, Alberta-
Some of my hon. friends will know him. This is one of the oases that I helped to adjust. This is a case again where the most misleading statements are made with respect to school land sales and taxes.

Robert Robertson, Lanark. Ontario-$357 refund due him re overpayment on sales 34313433.
This relates to section 11, township 10, range 6. east of the principal meridian, files 1338081-82-83 S.L.
This section was acquired by Mr. Robert Robertson by virtue of assignments registered from the former recorded holders.
The department made several demands from Mr. Robertson for payment of the arrears and in 1919 he communicated with the department, pointing out that owing to the war and the moratorium, he was unable to collect moneys due him. therefore was not in a position to reduce the indebtedness.
In 1922 he filed a declaration that he had erected on the lands very substantial improvements.	In March, 1924, Mr. Robertson
approached the department, requesting that he be permitted to surrender his interest in the sales comprising the east half of the section, and have the moneys paid by him applied on account of the purchase price of the west half, and Mr. Robertson represented at the time that he was about 80 years of age and that he was desirous of cleaning up all matters of this nature before he passed away. Representations were also made on his behalf by other interested parties, and in view of the proposed amendment to the Dominion Lands Act to provide for consolidation of sales, the department agreed to grant the request of Mr. Robertson, but it was clearly understood that no refund would be made of any moneys after consolidation had taken place.
After we had made the necessary adjustments and cancelled the sales comprising the east half of the section, it was found that there was a credit balance of $357.44, which money was retained by the department.
As Mr. Robertson agreed to the consolidation under the conditions set out by the department, I claim that he is not entitled to any refund. In this case I would also draw your attention to memorandum of the 13th ultimo addressed to you by Mr. Stafford.
Refund Case 5
W. S. Featherstonaugh-$238 refund due him on account overpayment on sale 3818-file 79720.
This relates to the northeast quarter of section 29. township 32, range 4, west of the 2nd meridian, file 79720 S.L.
In regard thereto I might state that Robert W. Cumming acquired this land at Canora, Saskatchewan, by purchase at public auction on the 4th November, 1912.
In February, 1914, Messrs. Langworthy and MeComber, barristers, of Port Arthur, advised the department that their client. William S. Fetherstonhaugh of Cochrane, Ontario, had acquired this land from Mr. Cumming, and under date of the 12th March. 1914, the writers were advised that in order for Mr. Fetherstonhaugh to be recognized by the

department it would be necessary to file a quit claim deed from Mr. Cumming to himself and have same registered in the department.
Several demands were made from Cumming, the recorded holder of the land, for payment of the arrears, and in October, 1918, we received a further letter from Messrs. Langworthy and MeComber advising that they were forwarding a quit claim deed from Cumming to Fetherstonhaugh; that Mr. Fetherstonhaugh was a civil engineer and was away on some work, and that it would be some little time before they could get in touch with him.
In October, 1918, we advised the writers that they should file with the department the quit claim deed in their possession in order that the advisability of recording Fetherstonhaugh as the holder of the land might be considered.
In reply the writers advised the department that Mr. Fetherstonhaugh had been at the front with the Canadian forces for some considerable time, and that they were endeavouring to locate him in France and would communicate with the department further at a latter date.
In November, 1918, Messrs. Langworthy and MeComber submitted for consideration an assignment from Cumming to Fetherstonhaugh, but as this was not properly executed and as further documents were required, the assignment was not registered at the time.
Numerous communications passed between the department and the interested parties in regard to the transfer of this land and in January, 1920, Mr. Fetherstonhaugh signed an agreement to pay 7 per cent on ail arrears of principal and interest.
In January, 1920, Messrs. Boland and Cumming, barristers, of Yorkton, forwarded a quit claim deed in favour of Mr. Fetherstonhaugh, which was registered in the department on the 18th June, 1920.
Mr. Fethersonhaugh does not appear to have made any representations to the department for a reduction in the rate of interest charged in view of his services overseas, and had he done so his request in all likelihood would have been refused, as he did not come into possession of the land in so far as the department is concerned, until the year 1920. Mr. Fetherstonhaugh failed to make any payments on account for a considerable length of time and in view of the representations made to the department to the effect that he was not living in the district, but was residing at Calary, Alberta, we granted him an extension of time of thirty days from the 27th March last within which to make a substantial reduction in the indebtedness and we also instructed the agent of Dominion Lands at Prince Albert on the same date to have an inspector make an inspection of the land and report as to the improvements thereon and as to the advisability of cancelling the sale.
I want to make clear to the committee that we do not cancel these sales until every effort has been made and every opportunity given to the purchaser to make payments if it is at all possible for him to do so.

Refund Case 8
C.P.R. Company-$5,377 refund due the company (principal $3,073 plus 15 years interest $2,3041 on Sask. sale 4427-file 27012-fiat 272343 covering 13.65 acres land required for right-of-way for Weyburn-Lethbridge C.P.R. in 1913. This would appear to relate to right-of-way of the Canadian Pacific Railway through the south half and north west quarter of section 11, township 8, range 30, west of the 2nd Meridian, file 27012 S.L.
In regard to this case the Canadian Pacific Railway Company made application to acquire right-of-way in the above mentioned land in October 1912, and in view of their representations the land was offered for sale, subject to reservation of the areas required for right-of-way.
When the land was disposed of by sale the south east quarter brought $190.00 per acre, the south west quarter $375.00 per acre, and the north west quarter $215.00 per acre, and the department decided to dispose of the areas required by the railway company for right-of-way at the same prices as those obtained for the areas disposed of by sale at public auction.
Under date of the 21st November 1912 an order in council was passed granted authority to sell to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the areas required for right-of-way at the rates referred to above.
Messrs. Ewart, Scott, McLaren and Kelley, solicitors for the railway company, protested against the valuation, claiming that they were informed that the land was only worth $30.00 per acre as farm land, and that the increase was due to the fact that they had located terminals at this point and established a townsite there.
The matter was submitted for consideration by the late Mr. Checkley under date of the 27th December 1912, and it was ruled that the price as fixed by sale of balance of section must stand. The company, therefore, made payment of the required amount in May 1913, and patent issued for the areas taken by the company on the 27th June, 1913; therefore, the department does not owe the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the amount claimed by Mr. McClymont, and I claim that we were perfectly within our rights in charging the prices which we did for the rigt-of-way in this land even though the fact that the railway company established its terminal at the point did increase the value.
Now I have covered every case. I am prepared to make returns in connection with them, and my hon. friend will find from the files that these sales were made under those conditions. I may say that these are a sample of the charges that have been made by McClymont with respect to the hundred other matters which he mentions but which I have not the time to go into. I have referred to the hundred million dollars that was to be saved by the department. The fact remains that in all this controversy I have been bombarded with letters from McClymont that if I would give him a job in the department at

I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that the matter is worthy of further discussion.

The minister has stated, Mir. Chairman, that he understood I had seen Mr. MoClymont for possibly three hours. This is entirely incorrect. I think any man who 'has a grievance has a perfect right to go to a member of parliament, and the member should listen to him. I have seen this man. Personally I think the minister would have done well had he himself given him an interview eighteen months ago, and thus have avoided a lot of unpleasant advertising of the department. As to the man's having had a fair show at the inquiry held by Mr. Smith, in my opinion it would have been much better for the department itself and the country as a whole if the matter had been brought before the publie accounts committee instead of being dealt with in camera. I am informed that when the witness was giving some rather stinging evidence the reporter 
was instructed not to take it down. I shall be very glad to have the minister refute this if it is untrue, for certainly if my information is well founded the witness was not fairly treated. As I say, these charges, whether true or false, have been in circulation for a long time, and to those of us who take a pride in the department it is not pleasant to see such charges ignored. They should have been dealt with promptly. I have brought the matter up in a spirit of kindness, and I should have thought he would have been glad of the opportunity to dispose of them once for all; instead of that the minister apparently is peeved.

speechtext: The minister is not peeved.
