speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I cannot
state definitely that the reporter was instructed by the commissioner not to take down the evidence referred to, but I have seen no record of such instructions having been given. I have read some of the loose statements made by this man since the inquiry was held. May I say that after absenting himself for thirty days on the first occasion when he was let out, in order to' be fair to him the assistant deputy minister took him on for a further period as a temporary employee, by arrangement with the Civil Service Commission. But we could not put up with a man of his temperament, for apparently he does not wish to render the kind of service we expect from the civil service. I want to say here and now, Mr. Chairman, that no matter how much advertising anyone may direct against me or my department, I am prepared to meet any charges openly and fairly. I am not at all incensed because my hon. friend has brought the matter up, but I do say that had he carefully perused the evidence and secured from the department the information contained in the file, I think he would have satisfied himself that the charges were without foundation. I think anyone reading oarefully the statements appearing in this man's advertisements must reach the conclusion that the author himself has furnished a complete answer to every charge he has made. Far be it from me to deny a civil servant any right that belongs to him. He will always get justice from me. More than that, I shall be always ready to extend sympathy. But no department can

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
afford to carry a gentleman who has demonstrated himself such a trouble maker as Mr. McClymont has done during the past two or three years.

I do not wish to discuss
the case at all. I have listened to the minister's explanation and I have no quarrel with it. I do not know the facts. May I say, however, in the most generous spirit of which I am capable, that in appointing a commissioner it would be wise for the government, either the present or any other, to select someone who is beyond all possibility of being regarded as having political prejudice. I say nothing against Mr. Alexander Smith. I know him and I like him; I have not a word to say against him. But I understand that for many years he was an organizer for the Liberal party. While of course that reflects no discredit on him, at the same time it does not alter the fact that in the eyes of the public he will have a natural prejudice in favour of the party. The minister, in my opinion, should have appointed as commissioner one who could not by any stretch of the imagination be looked upon as being prejudiced. I am not saying that the commissioner in this instance was prejudiced, but I suggest that it would have been well to appoint someone who could not possibly be regarded as susceptible to prejudice-someone such as a judge, either of the county court or of any of the other courts-to inquire into the matter. The commissioner should be a man absolutely above political favouritism of any kind, and in that case his report would be accepted as being possibly more conclusive than the report of a commissioner who, as everyone knows, has been perhaps a pretty strong Liberal. Possibly I should say partisan instead. I make this statement with no disrespect to the present commissioner, but I suggest that it would have been wiser, and in the future it would be just as well, to appoint a judge to a position of this kind.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior

I don't care about that.

I have not had time to read over the report or the evidence connected therewith, nor have I had time to read all the advertisements in the newspapers. I should
be willing and ready to have the fullest investigation. Any time my hon. friends have had leisure to peruse this evidence, if there is anything in it which they feel needs investigation, the fullest opportunity will be given if I am here acting as minister.

I have no expectation that I shall find time to read it all although I might. My only reason for mentioning the matter at all is that it has received so much publicity, and there may be people in the community- as a matter of fact I personally know there are some-who think that parliament should investigate the matter. Personally I have not had the time to look into it and I simply ask the minister to give us this assurance. I am glad to have his statement on the matter.

Did that fellow Mc-
Clymont ask for $50,000 a year to save millions to the country?

I do not
know about $50,000 a year, but I believe that is the statement he made as to saving millions to the country.

I wish to ask the minister a question regarding the raising of buffalo. There are one or two ranchers in Saskatchewan whe have applied for some breeding stock. They are willing to comply with the regulations of the department if the government will grant them two or three buffalo as the foundation for a herd. What policy is the government following in this regard? Is it possible for these men to get one or two buffalo from Wainwright, seeing that they are overstocked on that farm?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Our policy
is this. If the individual or the municipality will guarantee that the buffalo will be cared for properly, and if proper facilities are provided to enable the public in the particular locality to see them, we give two animals free of charge from the station at Wainwright. The cost of shipping and the responsibility will be on the individual or the municipality to take them from that point to destination.
Will the minister explain the increase of $110,420 in this item?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to make a few
observations with respect to the McClymont matter. I read the report of Mr. Commissioner Smith, not very carefully but sufficiently so to enable me to speak by reference to it. The commissioner made certain recommendations. He states first of all that if the department could be consolidated in one large building it would permit of greater supervision and would cut down expenses by allowing certain services to be centralized which are now duplicated in different branches. After referring to the report of 1922 which dealt with the observatory, he goes further and states:
I find that the work of the department has not only greatly increased but that the nature of the same in many eases has changed considerably. I find that the reorganization plan prepared by officers of the department, and adopted in 1920 by the minister, which has as its main feature the consolidation of related services and the reduction thereby of a number of branches from over thirty to twelve, will ensure the most efficient and economical performance of the department's many and varied duties.
I gather from this that the recommendations of 1920 have not been effected; there has not been a reduction from thirty to twelve. The recommendations were made in the year preceding the advent of the present administration and would have been carried into effect had this government not succeeded. That is

Mr. Smith's report. Then he makes certain major recommendations to which I direct the attention of this committee.
I have two major recommendations which I respectfully submit for your consideration. I am personally satisfied that if they are adopted they will afford a further check on any tendency to extravagance that might arise in the department. These are:
1.	That a greater measure of responsibility should be placed upon the secretary of the department in the matter of deciding the necessity for equipment and supplies requisitioned by the various branches of the department.
2.	That, whereas it is understood that the financial controller scrutinizes minutely all accounts, it should be a standard principle of administration that the advice of the financial controller be sought by the branch heads before any expenditure is recommended.
That report was signed by Alexander Smith. I regard these observations of the commissioner, together with the two major recommendations to which he refers, as being of great public importance. It was established in the mind of the commissioner at least that so long ago as 1920 a considered plan for the reorgnization of the department had engaged the attention of its officials and had been accepted and adopted by the then minister and that that plan of reorganization contemplated a reduction in the number of branches, if I might use that word, from thirty to twelve, and further that with respect to the purchasing of supplies the public purse would be better safeguarded if the principles to which Mr. Smith refers were applied to those purchases.
I leave that with those observations, but it must be borne in mind that for a period of weeks Mr. McClymont has been publishing in a newspaper of this city certain charges against the administration of the Department of the Interior. My friend the Minister of the Interior is quite right when he says that these charges are not all directed against 'him, although his name is mentioned in some of them. He is quite correct in saying that they do not refer to one administration or to two administrations; they are general and refer to a long period of time, and may be summarized in the following terms:	First, he
charges that excessive prices are paid for supplies and that the system adopted for the purchase of supplies is wrong. I have satisfied myself that that can be substantiated and abundantly proven. I think it is clear that the methods adopted to-day by the Department of the Interior with respect to the purchasing of supplies are wrong, and that a body appointed by this parliament as purchasing agents, for which we are appropriating substantial sums of money, does not properly

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
function, because if they discharged their duties properly supplies for that department could be bought at much lower prices than are now paid. It is true that the prices are certified to by the Auditor General as being fair and reasonable; it is true that very often the prices are certified by the purchasing officer, whoever he may be, but the truth is that tenders are invited for supplies from a limited number of persons and that they fix the prices, which are out of all proportion to what the true prices should be. I say that, for instance, with respect to the national park near Calgary. A limited number of persons have their names placed upon a patronage list; that list is limited to a number of people who do a retail business and they are asked to supply soap, for instance, in large quantities. I know of a case in which a soap manufacturer, by accident seeing one of these advertisements, tendered for the amount required, but his deposit was returned to him. What is more, one of the superintendents of the park was told that he must consult with the defeated candidate before doing any particular thing with respect to the administration of that park. Then is it any wonder that officials make charges such as these? These are facts, not fancies, and I take it that that is the reason why Mr. Smith made the recommendations contained in his report.
I regard Mr. McClymont's very vague and general statements in the same way the minister regards them; he should not be charged with dereliction of duty in vague and general statements, it is true, but there are certain specific charges and one of them is that to which I have referred. I do say that I have satisfied myself from personal observation and investigation that these goods are not obtained for the lowest prices for which they could be purchased by the Department of the Interior or any of its branches; that favorites are chosen, political favorites, partisans, who may be doing retail business, for the purpose of supplying goods by wholesale. This does not apply only to the Department of the Interior; it applies to many other departments, to the Department of Public Works, for instance, and to other departments of the public service. This may have been the practice in this country before the war, but we did hope and believe that our experience with respect to purchasing commissions had been such as to end that sort of thing. Not only are goods purchased in the way I have described, but employment is given under conditions which I mentioned the other day. I read a letter to the committee, and my friend the Minister of Railways ad-56103-2431
mitted that the conditions to which I referred prevailed with respect to the Rideau canal. He was helpless at the moment to contend against those conditions. It is said that these conditions prevailed in 1911 and in 1912. It is true that these conditions did obtain in those years, but we did hope that by reason of the changed conditions in this country, by reason of the great burden of debt we are carrying and by reason of the necessity for the exercise of economy, this country would realize that we must get the most value possible for every dollar we spend. I say that is not being done in the public service at the present moment and that is one of the charges made by Mr. McClymont. Look at the estimates to-day; we find that a commission composed of two or three people have certain powers and obligations with respect to these matters.
The charges made by Mr. McClymont were first that there was not adequate supervision as to the quantity of supplies required and secondly that the financial controller did not exercise that control over these matters which he should exercise. Then what happens? We have Mr. Smith making these recommendations. These are his recommendations, and I am sure no one will charge Mr. Smith with having made these recommendations out of any great desire to find fault with a Liberal administration. In that regard I believe he was conscious of the necessity of greater carebeing exercised in the purchase of goods by public departments.
Then Mr. McClymont makes another charge; he charges that vast sums of money are being expended uselessly in Ottawa, and in the public press he gave his references to the cost of the maintenance of automobiles and the utilization of these automobiles by one particular family. He gave those particulars; are they true or are they not? If they are true, no officer of the department has a right to the use of a private automobile at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada, and we are told that the automobiles were used not for the purposes of public business but for the purpose of conveying him to and from his home and his place of business. If this sort of thing is to be done let it be done openly and frankly as a part of the conditions of his employment; if it is not to be done let us say so and let us stop it.
Mr. McCymont made other charges in connection with the administration of the school lands branch of the department and in connection with the sale of other parts of the public domain. With respect to that I qm'+r-

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
agree with the minister; these charges cover a very large number of cases; they cover lands in every part of the three western provinces and they cover contracts made with people in almost every part of the world. We have certain statutes in this country, and whether or not the terms of those statutes have been observed is a matter which should not be determined by this house in an hour, a day, a week or a month. These are matters of detail which require much examination and much consideration, but I have investigated two of these matters myself. Two of these charges concerned property near my community, one merely dealing with the sale of land to the town of Macleod and the other the sale of another small piece of land.
I think in that case the minister did what any minister would have done having regard to the conditions which prevailed in the town of Macleod, for instance, at that time. Macleod was a town which had made default, if I remember correctly, in connection with the payment of interest on its debentures. It had its power plant on a certain piece of land and had made default on the purchase price of the land. The minister put the land up for sale under conditions which ensured the town of being able to get this piece of land at about $20 an acre, which was more than it was worth at that time having regard to the conditions which prevailed in the town and as far as my knowledge goes it is more than it is worth at present. It seems to [DOT] me that is not a matter which should engage the attention of parliament at this time, but there are charges contained in these advertisements inserted by Mr. McClymont which reflect upon the civil service of the country and upon the administration of the Department of the Interior altogether apart from the minister, the departmental head. It seems to me that these charges make it incumbent that there should be some way by which those people who have read these advertisements in the newspaper may have their minds set at rest. That does not only apply to those of us in parliament; this newspaper has a wide circulation, and the advertisements have been read by large numbers of people. I have been asked what are we going to do about it, what the opposition propose to do. My answer is perfectly clear; no opposition and no member of parliament can undertake to deal with these questions, for the reasons which have been given by the minister. It does occur to me that there are reasons sufficiently strong in these advertisements to necessitate an inquiry by the public IMr. Bennett.]	:	; S
accounts committee with respect to the expenditure of public moneys for administration, the purchase of supplies, the payment of large living allowances, and matters of that kind. These are small matters and may look insignificant, but it only takes ten ten-dollar bills to make a hundred dollars, ten of those to make a thousand, and a thousand to make a million. We have got so much in the habit of talking loosely in thousands and millions that you would think this country was ready to hand out ten-dollar tips to waiters. That is not the sort of thing that should prevail, and I will give you an illustration of it.
I was told by a responsible minister of one of the greatest countries in the world that the head of his state had taken such an interest in the practice of economy, even in stationery and pencils, that they found it difficult sometimes to get along with their business. Friendly competitions had been invited among the representatives of that state in the various sections of the country with respect to pencils and stationery, and matters of that kind, which effected very great economy. Now, that all sounds piffle, and somebody says "Why should we waste the time of parliament about something like that?" But it was just that which made it possible for Mr. Coolidge to bring about the economy he did in the United States of America. Those who are interested and who will take the time to Tead what was said in the report in connection with the last budget regarding the savings accomplished by the methods I have indicated, will realize how desirable it is that we should look upon these matters in a different sense.
I am satisfied, from the evidence that I have read-I have not had time to read it carefully-and from reading these advertisements in a very casual way, that the money of this country is not being spent so as to get the largest possible value for every hundred cents that we take out of the exchequer. I am quite sure that the Prime Minister is anxious^ that this country's affairs should be economically conducted. It is not easy to do that, and nobody knows it better than I do. Nobody knows how difficult it is to ensure economical practice in the administration of the government and in the conduct of public affairs; we all know that. But where loose habits prevail; where the one who is in charge permits laxity to prevail, then you set up a condition whereby every man subordinate in position thinks it is his bounden duty to imitate his superior, and the result is that you have vast expenditures. I think it is to this that Mr. Smith refers in the last two paragraphs of his report.

First of all he mentions reorganization and consolidation of services, and the removal of a number of branches. Then he recommended imposing upon the secretary of the department the duties and functions of his office, and the supervision by the financial comptroller of all accounts, to bring about the results so much to be desired.
It will be borne in mind that the main document of nineteen pages upon which Mr. Smith predicates his final report against Mc-Clymont is one which was issued in 1922, and had to deal with the late Doctor Klotz of the observatory. That is the main document upon which the major part of his findings were predicated.
It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that while this committee cannot possibly investigate this matter and go into all these charges-if the word "charges" might be used -they are of such a serious character, not with respect to the minister but with respect to the conduct of the public service of Canada, as to require a full investigation before a special or standing committee of this house. It should be taken up at the very beginning of the session and carried through to the end, in order that those who have served the state faithfully, for a long period of years may be relieved of any odium that may be attached to them if they are innocent, and those punished who are found to be guilty. With the work we have had this session we have not had the opportunity to do any more than just look at this in a casual sort of way, but if we could call for the various files that may be concerned, we would be able to deal with it as it should be dealt with.
I heartily agree with the minister on the question of employment. No department could continue to employ one who has made charges of this character in the public press; it would be incompatible and inconsistent with the whole theory of public service that it should be done. I, for one, heartily support the minister in the view he takes, but it is hardly a fair assumption to say that all this has been done, all these sums of money have been expended by an individual merely for the purpose of trying to get back a job. Elementary intelligence would indicate to him that he could not possibly hope to get back his position after having gone through the ordeal that he did with respect to the investigation, or having made the charges which he has made in the public press. I quite agree with that, but I do think there still is left that residuum which necessitates the minister taking such steps as may be necessary to see that the
public service is vindicated and finding out if there is any foundation at all for what has been said. I cannot but think that there is some foundation, or Mr. Smith would not have made the observations he did.

I have been trying to get the floor for some time, after listening to this discussion which has been under way for almost an hour. I want to introduce a new subject, and that is the question of clearing land by fire. I should like to read this letter which appears in a return to an order of the house dated February 13, 1928. It is a letter to Mr. Wilson, of Peace River, signed by the Deputy Minister of the Interior, and is dated June 1, 1926. It reads:
I have your letter of the 12th April last, in which you request that a small grant be made to Mr. De Bolt for the purpose of enabling him to burn off a considerable acreage of bush land to facilitate settlement.
I am afraid it will be impossible to authorize any burning operations, save under strict departmental control. You will understand that if the grant were made to Mr. De Bolt, or any one else, and any damage resulted from the burning operations, the department would be held liable. This fact alone makes it necessary to impose the fundamental requirement that any burning operations must be strictly under the control of qualified officers of the department.
In addition, the report of Mr. Lonergan, Inspector of Surveys, which you quote, stresses the point that fire guards must be put in the first thing in the spring and burning done as early in the season as possible, because otherwise there is danger of damage to the soil itself. Unfortunately, for this year at least, the season in the west opened so early as to make it impossible to organize operations for this year.
The matter will be kept in mind, however, and I hope it will be possible to make arrangements to proceed with further experimental burning operations in the spring of 1927.

I would ask if it is the intention to go ahead with these burning experiments or operations during this year or in the spring of next year, and what the policy of the department is in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The burning operations conducted in that locality some four or five years ago were apparently successful. I would hardly agree with the statement contained in the letter that we would not allow anyone else to burn on crown lands, because these are crown lands. First of all they have to be fire guarded for a respectable width in order to prevent the fire escaping, and the burning has to be done at a period of the year when the surface soil will not bum so that a good deal of care must be exercised. I really must say that I do not believe it is the duty of the government to do this work on a very large scale. We have carried out one experiment and have demonstrated what can be done. I am quite prepared, if the necessity arises and it is desirable to do so, to render some assistance to the settlers themselves. I think they can do it more acceptably than anyone else when they go in upon these lands. I know my hon. friend has in mind the burning off of half a township that would open up that land at once and make it more or less prairie land. We have carried out one experiment, and we do not feel that we should continue this kind of thing indefinitely.

In view of the fact that some of the northern territories are being settled in spite of anything governments do or do not do, we ought to give this matter careful consideration, and I think it would be wise to go ahead and actually clear this land by fire. It seems to me ridiculous to be discussing settlement schemes in this house which contemplate the advancing of money or other assistance to clear land at a cost of upwards of $30 an acre, when the Department of the Interior through its own officials has demonstrated that this land can be cleared for less than $1 an acre.

Is the hon. member really serious in making that statement? If so, I would like him to state the type of land that can be cleared for less than $1 an acre, the kind of wood that is on it, its size and thickness.

Land that would cost from $30 to $50 an acre to clear by hand was cleared by departmental surveyors for less than $1 an acre. That is the statement, and I can prove it if the hon. member wants me to take up the time of the committee.

Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
But suppose the figures are $15 and $5, where is the economy from the national standpoint in asking a settler to waste his time clearing land by hand which could be cleared for one-tenth or one-twentieth of the cost in a systematic way by government officials or others? When the minister takes the stand that he is prepared to assist the settler, I would point out that the land cannot foe cleared economically by that method, because you cannot follow the natural boundaries in providing fire guards. If you are going to guard against the fire getting away, it is necessary to take the open spots through bush land in order to get the proper fire guards, and you cannot follow the section or township lines. It seems to me the Department of the Interior could serve a very useful purpose by taking hold of this proposition. One of the great difficulties we have to-day in the province of Alberta, as the minister knows, is to supply transportation to outlying settlements. In some instances you have a strip of prairie, then a strip of bush land, the settlers do not care to take that up even if it is within ten or fifteen or forty miles of a railway, and the result is that they go back one hundred miles. In another five years there will be a demand from these settlers for two or three hundred miles of railway construction, even though they could have taken up land lying within twenty or thirty miles of a railway, but they preferred the land further back because it had been cleared by fire possibly set by somebody in a careless moment. I think the minister has lost a good opportunity to prevent the development in the next few years of a serious problem in connection with the providing of transportation facilities in the Peace River country at least, and possibly in northern Saskatchewan, by not undertaking this work.

In view of what the hon. member has just told the committee, I think I should carry the matter a little further. I remember last year an inquiry was held by the railway and canals committee regarding transportation in the Peace River country, and a certain civil servant was brought in to the committee by, I believe, the hon. member for Peace River, who told us in that committee that it would cost not mpre than 15 cents an acre to set fires under certain satisfactory conditions. But to set fires costing 15 cents an acre is not clearing land. He told us further that the timber in that country was large and heavy, and that there was much of it. Everyone knows the type of land where the bush grows thick enough and large enough, and no grass or underbrush grows sufficient to fire except in dry times. If a man sets out a fire in those dry times it can
certainly be done cheap enough. I do not know why the price was set at 15 cents an acre. A single match from a box of the high-class matches we get across the river would set out a fire, and I do not know why the price was set so high. The member for Peace River I notice has the price elevated a little more. But when the witness was asked what it would cost to chop down the trunks and -pick up the stumps and burn them, he said, "Oh, the farmer -must do that himself." There is a good deal of experimental work being carried on as to the best and cheapest and quickest way of clearing land, but certainly it would not be a good thing for the minister of the interior to allow any of his men to spend much time or money setting out fires. It is very difficult at times to get a fire to run at all in heavy poplar brush, for there is nothing in the bottom to burn. The better way is to cut down the stuff that is not too large, by using a scrub cutter, and in smaller growth modern -tractors can plough the stuff down and in a few years it rots; but simply to set out fires is very far from making land fit to cultivate.

I think my hon. friend
has not had much experience with this class of land.

I am actually
engaged in clearing land where the poplar timber runs up to two feet in thickness at the stump and stands rather thick, and it is very difficult to get a fire to burn throught it. I have been trying for years to bum up the trunks. If the hon. member for Peace River could tell me where I could get the services of a civil servant to clear my land at a dollar an acre after the stumps are out of the ground, I would thank him very much for the information.

I wish to put two letters on Hansard. One is dated February 25, 1927, and is to Mr. Peters, surveyor general, who was called before the committee last year. I wrote his as follows:
Dear Sir,
Some years ago your department undertook to test out the feasibility of clearing land by fire. I have been urging on the minister occasionally the desirability of doing a little more at this business as we have vast areas in the Peace river country that can be cleared economically by fire without doing any damage. I would like to obtain the following information:
1.	What areas or sections were cleared by fire during the progress of the whole experiment?
2.	What was the effect of the experiment in relation to clearing the land?
3.	Was the soil damaged in any way?
4.	What was the cost per acre of clearing the land?
3850	COMMONS
Supply-Interior-Dominion Lands
5.	Was there any difficulty controlling the fire?
6.	In what years was the experiment carried on?
7.	Has the land been settled since it was cleared?
An answer to these questions, will greatly oblige.
This is the reply I received from him:
Dear Mr. Kennedy,
Referring to your letter of February 25th concerning the clearing of land by controlled firing in the Peace river country. Answering your questions under the same numbers, I would say,
1.	Area No. 1, comprising sections 27, 28, 33 and 34, in township 76, range 21, west of the fifth meridian, which is a short distance south of Donnelly on the E. D. & B. C. railway, and area No. 3, comprising about 90,000 acres in the vicinity of Battle River prairie (a map is attached outlining this area).
2.	In areas 1 and 3 good burns were obtained and the experiment was a success.
3.	The firing was done in the spring of the year and the soil was not damaged in any way.
4.	In area No. 1 the area was so small that the cost per acre would not be typical. In area No. 3 the cost was about three cents per acre. It is probable that the cost for each burn might vary from three cents up to fifteen cents per acre according to the facilities for natural fire guards and other conditions of a like nature.
5.	The fires can be controlled, provided the work is done under proper supervision and the necessary precautions are taken.
6.	Area No. 1 was burned in 1919. In 1920 an experiment was tried in burning an area of approximately 25 acres ten to fifteen miles southeast of the town of Peace river, and another party undertook firing operations near the Bad Heart river, northeast of Grande Prairie. Because of adverse weather conditions the work of this season was not a success. Area No. 3 was burned in 1921.
7.	I regret that we have no information as to settlement of the land that has taken place subsequently, but no doubt you can obtain this information readily from another branch of the department.
From this letter it is apparent that the clearing of land by controlled firing was a success. Regardless of the proportion of the clearing done, my information is that it can be carried out by the department very cheaply in comparison with what it would cost an actual settler to do. I do not see how the Minister of Immigration can justify the policy which subsidizes the bringing in of settlers and burning them loose on farms where it costs them $35 an acre to clear land, if this work can be done for 15 or 30 cents or a dollar an acre by controlled firing by the government. Would it not be better to subsidize the clearing of land in this way than to bring out settlers to waste their lives cutting down bush? The hon. member challenged the success of this operation, but territory was cleared by fire one hundred, miles north of the Peace river, and to-day settlers are going back there
fMr. Kennedy.]
rather than settle half that distance from the railway. That seems to me to be a practical answer to his light manner of dealing with the whole question, waving it aside as being something of no value.

It is possible
that settlers will go further back to land burnt over some years ago; but when the Department of the Interior is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to fight fires, I am surprised that the hon. member for Peace River should ask him to set out fires in woods which in a comparatively short time may become valuable. The fact remains that the gentleman who gave evidence before the committee last year and said it cost 15 cents an acre to clear land by firing, still maintains that the farmer must at his own expense gather up the trunks and stumps and bum them. Scores of members from the eastern provinces and the western know that there is a great deal better way of clearing land than by firing. I asked the hon. member as to the size of the wood in this case, but he did not tell me. I asked the witness last year, and he said it was quite large timber. Large green stumps will not bum if the fire passes over them quickly. If they are burned again and again it is easier for the settlers to clear the land.
The hon. member persists in handing out information which may apply to his own district,-
It applies to any heavily timbered district.

-but when he says we are advocating lighting fires, while the department is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting fires, I want to tell him that the problem here is between controlled fires and fires not controlled. If the firing is done intelligently under the control of the departmental officials the soil will not be damaged and the fire will not destroy good timber. Further, there will not be the temptation for settlers to start fires and thereby destroy indiscriminately poor timber and good timber. It seems to me that the policy is a^good one from whatever angle it may be studied. It has been argued by some officials, and even by the minister and the hon. member for Melfort, that firing will destroy the soil. Now, in 1023 I know a certain area was fired in the West-lock district. Two years afterwards in that very area there were splendid crops yielding a hundred bushels to the acre on that burnt land. So the statement that the soil is destroyed is not borne out by my experience, and I have watched a lot of firing in the Peace River country. If fire is properly

controlled it will do effective work and will not damage the soil or affect adversely the general interests of the country. On the other hand it will enable settlers to establish themselves on the land much sooner and to some extent obviate the transportation difficulties we have experienced in connection with railways and new roads throughout the province of Alberta in the last five, six or ten years.

The minister will recall that two years ago the hon. member for Vancouver Centre raised a question with respect to alienation of water powers in the Rocky mountains park. It was felt that under the circumstances, without the consent of parliament, these water powers should not be alienated. The attitude taken by this government in recent years has been that they are really trustees for the western provinces, having regard to the fact that the resources are to be turned over to those provinces at no
distant date. There is pending an application in connection with the water power in Manitoba, and I do suggest to the minister, having regard to the fact that this parliament -not the minister or the government but parliament itself-is the trustee for the western provinces, to whom these resources will at no distant date be turned over, that the government should decline to part with any of these power sites, which are of inestimable value to the people of the west, until such time at least as parliament-not, I repeat, the ministry-has passed upon the transaction. I look upon this as an entirely different matter from water powers entrusted to the government for administration. These water powers, whatever else may be said, are now merely held in trust for people residing at a distance from us; and inasmuch as the legislature of Manitoba, for example, is not in session, it does occur to me that before any action is taken the approval of this parliament should be given. I cannot think that this is a matter for executive action alone. I cannot think that it is fair or just or right that this ministry or any ministiy at this moment should deal wth the matter in this way. The responsibility will always be laid at the door of this parliament in years to come; when the situation becomes acute and difficulties arise it will be said that we were responsible for the action taken.
I know the minister has taken a strong view with respect to some matters in my own province, and in view of the facts that have been brought to my attention I suggest that he give the house an assurance that no water powers in western Canada will be alienated without the approval of parliament; because no other action will meet the situation adequately at this time. If the legislatures of the provinces desire to alienate these powers when they receive them, well and good, that is a matter with respect to which they can formulate policies. But in view of the present condition, in view of the negotiations that are taking place, the fact that in one province an agreement was actually signed, while in another province proposals have been made which have been stated to be acceptable-in view of these circumstances, I submit that we should not part with these very valuable power sites, with all that is involved for the future population of the western provinces. We should not part with these powers without the consent of parliament. And that consent probably could not be given unless the legislatures of the provinces affected were content; because there

is a point at which executive action, taken by a government which in one sense has no responsibility while in another sense it has considerable, is not the method which in my opinion was contemplated when the statute was framed. It was contemplated then that we should treat these matters as part of the assets of the Dominion; now we are content to regard them as assets in our hands as trustees. I make that suggestion to the minister in view of the position he took some years ago with respect to another matter Rather than move a motion on going into supply, which would involve the necessity of a vote being taken, I bring the matter to his attention now in order that he may consider it before he finally disposes of this item.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
quite take the view expressed by my hon. friend with respect to trusteeship in connection with these natural resources. The natural resources are the property of the federal government; that cannot be denied. I think my hon. friend will admit that at once. If parliament in its wisdom decides to turn the natural resources back to the provinces, then that is the business of parliament. But while the resources are under the control of the federal government they are under the administration and control of the federal authorities. There is some difference between the situation which my hon. friend has stated and the position I took on this matter a year or two ago. The matter was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, but it had reference to the alienation of water powers within the parks. The suggestion- at that time was that the parks and all that appertains thereto, inasmuch as they were recreational grounds not only for tihe localities in which they were located, but for the whole of Canada, should not be alienated but be put under the control of parliament. I heartily agreed with that suggestion. So far as Banff and the Spray lakes scheme are concerned, we have been resurveying the park with a view to excluding from the park area all the valuable minerals now known to exist within the park boundaries. The park boundaries will be curtailed to some extent and most of the coal areas will now be outside their limits and in the Rocky mountain forest reserve. The suggestion was made to exclude the Spray lakes. Let me say this with respect to the Spray lakes. We must have a dependable flow into the Spray river, particularly during the tourist season; and the engineer of the Calgary Power Company, Mr. Gahertv informed

me in my office not long ago that if we were to take for that purpose more than 150 cubic second feet during three months even, in the tourist season, they were not at all interested in that development. I am glad to get that admission. We shall need in the neighbourhood of 350 to 400 cubic second feet to preserve the scenic qualities of the river, to have sufficient water for fire protection, and for the purposes necessary for the maintenance of the park and the preservation of its beauty. But when my hon. friend separates the water powers from the other natural resources-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Oh, no; they are the
same thing.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am willing to admit that they are valuable; so much so that I am exercising extreme caution in their administration. I think my hon. friend will give me credit for that, because we have had innumerable difficulties on the Winnipeg river where the Seven Sisters falls are located, and to date, I think, the disposition of these water powers has met with universal satisfaction. Now I understand my hon. friend to say that if I give a promise that no disposition of any water power will be made until it is placed under the control of-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
What did
my hon. friend say?

I quite appreciate the protection given a minister in securing the consent of parliament to any question which involves such an important decision as that of the disposal of 300,000 horse power, but I do say that Manitoba has been the storm centre ever since I came to this government and was honoured with the control of the Department of the Interior; first over the Norman dam, later over the disposition of the pulpwood berth where the mill is now erected and the disposition of the water power, and now a very grave difference of opinion exists with respect to the disposition of the Seven Sisters

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am sure the committee appreciated the statement made by the minister, but I think he did not entirely grasp my contention with respect to the trusteeship of this parliament. So long as we held the natural resources without having declared as a policy that we proposed to turn them over to the provinces; so long as we did not declare that policy his position was sound, but at the beginning of last session and reiterated again this session we had the policy declared that it is proposed to transfer these resources to the several provinces, and the agreement was actually signed and executed which would turn the resources over to the province of Alberta. Under these circumstances, in view of the statement made by the Prime Minister that it was proposed immediately after prorogation or as soon thereafter as might be reasonable to carry on the negotiations to a completion or until they failed, I submit that we should no longer treat these resources as the property of the crown in the right of the Dominion but as the property of the crown in trust for the crown, in the right of the provinces. That is the point I desire to make, and the last observation made by the minister somewhat supports the view which I was presenting. The position of the parks was not so strong as the case which I now put, for with respect to the parks it was proposed that they should always remain the property of the crown in the right of the Dominion and therefore the Dominion had complete authority to deal with them, having complete authority to deal with them the minister concluded that it was desirable to have the approval of parliament before there was any alienation of any resources within the parks.
My submission is that since we hold these resources, that is, they are the property of the crown in the right of the Dominion, in trust for the crown in the right of the several provinces, we should not as an executive act or as a pure matter of administration part with so valuable a resource as a power site which is of such inestimable value to the people of the country, without the approval of this parliament. In my judgment that would be a proper release to the minister for any action he might take as trustee for the people affected, and would afford an opportunity to the several legislatures to deal with any matter which concerned them until such time
as these resources, notably the power sites, were turned over to the crown in the right of the several provinces concerned.
I trust that I have made myself clear; I did not develop the matter at first because I thought the minister had that position in mind. I quite agree that the minister should not be asked at the moment to state what might be done, but thinking the matter over while I was away last week, rather than propose an amendment to the motion to go into supply for the purpose of discussion I thought I could present the matter in that way when his estimates were under consideration, and I thought he might take some little time to consider what might be desirable in the premises because his statement indicates a very earnest desire on his part to deal with the matter in the sense I have suggested, the sense of the relations and obligations which this parliament bears not only to this generation but, as he says, to the future, having regard to the fact that 300,000 horse power may be affected. The same principle, of course, applies to the White Mud falls. Possibly the minister would leave one item, purely pro forma, in order that it might be spoken to, and he might be good enough to present his views to-morrow or at some later time and thereby possibly prevent any further discussion on the matter.

Amount not exceeding $39,000,000 to meet expenditures made or indebtedness incurred (where amounts available from net operating income or investments may be insufficient) by or on behalf of the Canadian National Railway Company, herein called "the company," or any company specified or referred to in chapter 172 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, and chapter 13 of the statutes of 1920 or now or hereafter comprised in the Canadian National Railways or by the company in respect of any railways, properties and works entrusted to it from time to time under the provisions of section 19 of chapter 172 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, or any one or more of such companies, on any or all of the following accounts, such expenditures or indebtedness being herein called authorized expenditures:
(a)	Interest on securities, notes and other obligations; rentals for lease of lines;
(b)	Equipment principal payments; sinking funds; miscellaneous maturing or matured notes and other obligations secured or unsecured; _
(c)	Operating income deficit, whenever incurred or ascertained;
(d)	construction and betterments, including co-ordinations.; acquisition of real or personal property.
The amount herein authorized may be applied from time to time to meet authorized expenditures, in the discretion of the governor in council:	_
(a)	In respect of railways, properties and works entrusted to the company as aforesaid;

(b)	In respect of railways, properties and works not so entrusted by way of loans in cash, or by way of guarantee, or partly one way and partly the other, subject, however, as follows:
If by way of loans from His Majesty, the amount or amounts advanced to any one or more of the said companies shall be repayable on demand, with interest payable half-yearly at the rate fixed from time to time by the governor in council, secured if and when directed by the governor in council by mortgage or mortgages upon such properties, in such form and containing such terms and conditions, not inconsistent herewith, as the governor in council may approve.
If by way of loans from persons other than His Majesty (without the guarantee^ of His Majesty) the amounts, terms and conditions of such loans shall be such as the governor in council may from time to time approve.
If by way of guarantee, any such guarantee may be either a general guarantee covering the total amount of the issue, or by a separate guarantee endorsed on each obligation, and may be of the principal, interest and sinking funds (if any) of the notes, obligations or securities of one or more of the said companies specified by the governor in council, which notes, obligations or securities the companies so_ specified are hereby authorized to make and issue, _ and such guarantee may be signed by the Minister of Finance, or such other person as the governor in council may authorize, on behalf of His Majesty, in such form and on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine to be appropriate and applicable thereto. Any guarantee so signed shall be conclusive evidence for all purposes that the provisions of this enactment have been complied with.
Should temporary loans be made or negotiated before the lapse of this appropriation either from His Majesty or other persons, guaranteed notes, obligations or securities may subsequently be issued under the provisions of the preceding paragraph of this enactment to renew, refund or adjust such loans, or any part thereof.	_
Each company herein mentioned or referred to is hereby authorized to aid and assist in any manner any other or others of the said companies, and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may for its own requirements and also for the requirements of any or all of such other companies from time to time:
(a)	Issue notes, obligations or other securities, joint or several, at discretion, for the purpose of any guarantee made or to be made under the provisions of this enactment;
(b)	Apply the proceeds of any such guaranteed issue, or the amount of loans received, by virtue of this enactment, in meeting authorized expenditures on its own account or on account of any or all of such other companies;
(c)	Make advances for the purpose of meeting authorized expenditures to any or all of such other companies, upon or without any security, at discretion.
No purchaser of such guaranteed notes, securities or obligations shall be under any obligation to inquire into the application of the proceeds of any guaranteed issue, $39,000,000.

Mr. MiacDONALD (South Cape Breton): I want to make a suggestion to the government in the hope of relieving the situation at Halifax. The situation as it appears to me is this. It is evidently going to cost the country about a million dollars to free Sir Henry Thornton from a position into which he has rather manoeuvred himself or allowed others to manoeuvre him. He is asking for a million dollars to build in Halifax an hotel for which there is absolutely no necessity. There are now three or four fairly good hotels at Halifax sufficient to answer all the requirements there. You can visit Halifax at any time of the year and you will find there hotels not at all crowded. In addition to that we are building a new community hotel which will of course take the cream of the traffic: it will be more than sufficient to accommodate all the tourist traffic for a considerable time to come. There has been an effort in the past year in Nova Scotia to stimulate the tourist traffic. The provincial government is spending a great deal of money, and many towns and cities throughout the province are also contributing to this move. In Cape Breton we have organized a regular tourist association, to which all towns and cities in the island have contributed. It is costing a considerable sum of money. I have here a piece of literature which has been distributed by the Tourist Association of Cape Breton. One great obstacle in the way of
tourist traffic throughout Nova Scotia is the want of good hotels, and for this million dollars for an hotel in Halifax-an hotel which is not needed-at least four or five good hotels could be constructed throughout the province. I have read the statement of President Beatty regarding the offer he makes with apparent generosity; but everyone who knows anything knows that Sir Henry Thornton cannot accept that offer. To do so would be at least a distinct Loss of prestige to him. He has taken a stand on the matter and he must maintain it. In fairness to him I think the alternative proposition should be made. The minister might vote this amount for the construction of hotels in Nova Scotia, and if Sir Henry Thornton then insisted on the hotel in Halifax, I do not think there is anything we could say about it. But it might commend itself to his good judgment to adopt the suggestion made by all the tourist associations throughout the province, and instead of building one hotel in Halifax he might build four or five throughout the province.
I have here a pamphlet issued by the Cape Breton Tourist Association, a very creditable publication entailing considerable expense, in which are set forth all the beauties of the island of Cape Breton. It is unnecessary to say that the island of Cape Breton is by far the most beautiful portion of all Canada. In support of that statement I might read a number of selections from this book but I will content myself with quoting just one from a very well known author, Charles Dudley Warner, whose writings are no doubt familiar to hon. members. Charles Dudley Warner visited the island of Cape Breton some thirty and forty years ago, long before the present transportation facilities were afforded, and he writes:
One seeing Baddeck would not like to be detained a prisoner in Eden. . . winding around the base of a wooded range, and crossing its point, we came upon a sight that took all the sleep out of us. This was the famous Bras d'Or . . . The scene was enchanting... It was enough to sit on deck forward of the wheel-house, and absorb, by all the sense, the delicious day. With such wonder perpetual and such scenery always present, sin in this world would soon become an impossibility The most electric American, heir of all the nervous diseases of all the ages, could not but find peace in this scene of tranquil beauty, and sail on into a great and deepening contentment. Would the voyage could last for an age, with the same sparkling, but tranquil, sea, and the same environment of hills, near and remote. The hills approached and fell away in lines of undulating grace, draped with tender colour -which helped to carry the imagination beyond the earth.
I would not suggest in all seriousness that there is no such thing as sin in the island

Seriously, however, I want to leave this suggestion with the minister, and I hope to receive the assistance of the Minister of National Defence, because I think it will commend itself to his good judgment. Instead of making this apply only to the city of Halifax it should apply to the province of Nova Beotia, so that if the president of the Canadian National Railways can see his way clear to do so he may confer a favour upon that province which will not be forgotten.

I submit that that is
not the proper way in which the House of Commons should deal with this matter, and for that Statement I will give my reasons shortly. The statute provides that the Minister of Railways represents the shareholders of this enterprise; the directors are appointed by the government and have the powers which appertain to statutory directors. They have the powers of directors under the Railway Act. The Canadian National Railways may be considered for that purpose to be a corporation, and the directors have control of that corporation in the same manner and to the same extent that directors have control of any private corporation. However, in every private corporation there are obligations placed upon the shareholders. These are statutory obligations; they arise under the act incorporating the company on the one hand, and under the general Railway Act on the other. The act of incorporation provides a limitation upon the powers of the directors and states clearly where the powers of the shareholders begin; that is, there are certain matters which may not be disposed of by the directors without reference to the shareholders, and the general Railway Act also provides that while the powers of the directors are very large in many instances, the directors must also refer matters of importance to the shareholders. These provisions apply to this undertaking. It is true that the Canadian National railways are owned by the people of Canada.

Now I submit that the proper form in which these estimates should be introduced would be by a separate bill, because in no sense can this be said to be supply. This is not supply; it is not money granted to His Majesty, and should not be treated in that way. It will be observed that we are treating these estimates as supply, and I submit to the ministei that by	no	stretch of	the imagination	can	hetreat these advances made to the corporation to which I have referred as supply granted to	His	Majesty.	The very term	"supplygranted	to His Majesty" involves	and	implies that we are raising by taxation sums of money to enable His Majesty's government to be maintained and to function. If my premise is correct this is a corporation; the government have a board of directors, subject to	the	provisions	of that general	act	and
with the additional provisions to which I have referred in the act incorporating the enterprise, and to which I will not refer now. However, if my premise be correct and I think the minister must admit, from his observations, that it is-we should not be treating these matters as supply. As I say, we should treat them as we treated the grants made to the harbours of Quebec, St. John and Halifax. They constitute an appropriation made out of the public revenues for specific purposes not related to supply, and they are improperly dealt with in the estimates.
The minister will say that heretofore these matters have been dealt with in this way. I have had occasion to look into this matter with some care since last year, and the conclusion at which I have arrived is embodied in the observations I have just made. I cannot help thinking that it must commend itself to the good judgment of the Minister of Railways that we should deal with these questions as matters of legislation which leaves the house much more free to deal with the situation than otherwise would be the case.
Now let me go a step further. If we are to deal with these matters as I have indicated, and going on the assumption that the management of the railway company, that is the directors, have recommended to the shareholders that they as shareholders appropriate sums necessary to maintain, develop and extend the property where necessary and to preserve it in its entirety, these items then represent recommendations made by the directors to the shareholders. Under the statute the Minister of Railways is the shareholder representing the people of Canada; the members of this house are really the shareholders in fact, because the minister derives his power from them, and I submit that it is still clearer than ever that this is not supply in any sense in which that term can be properly used.
